patient.name: Opal Henley
dx: Chronic venous insufficiency, bilateral lower extremities
Venous stasis ulcer, left medial lower leg

radiology.study: Venous duplex ultrasound, left lower extremity
radiology.finding: Great saphenous vein reflux 1.8 s; deep venous system patent, no DVT

patient.wound_dressing: Multilayer compression wrap (Profore), changed weekly; foam primary dressing
patient.clinical_notes: 71-year-old female with chronic venous insufficiency, seen for follow-up of a non-healing left medial lower-leg ulcer first documented 03/02/2026 (now ~14 weeks). Exam: ulcer over the medial gaiter region with an irregular, shallow border, ruddy granular base, scant serous exudate, and no necrotic tissue. Surrounding skin shows hemosiderin staining and lipodermatosclerosis; 2+ pitting edema; visible varicosities. Venous duplex on 03/09/2026 confirmed great saphenous reflux. CEAP class C6; VCSS 12. Multilayer compression initiated 03/16/2026 with weekly changes plus leg elevation; over more than 4 weeks of standard care the wound shows less than 50% (<50%) area reduction. Wound is clean, granular, and greater than 1 cm². Plan: continue compression; team discussing cellular/tissue product (skin substitute) application at the next visit. No ankle-brachial index (ABI), toe pressures, or pedal pulse exam are recorded in the chart.

venous_reflux_studies.evidence: Venous duplex 03/09/2026 — great saphenous reflux confirms venous stasis.

abi_supports_venous.evidence: No ABI, TBI, toe pressure, or pedal-pulse exam on file — perfusion is unconfirmed, and an ABI ≤0.9 would flip the etiology toward arterial/mixed.

compression_appropriate_for_abi.evidence: Compression is running with no ABI on file. Per P&P it is contraindicated below 0.60 — appropriateness and safety cannot be certified without the number.

edema_managed.evidence: 2+ pitting edema addressed with compression plus leg elevation.

ceap_vcss.evidence: CEAP class C6 and VCSS 12 documented.

wound_characteristics_venous.evidence: Medial gaiter location, hemosiderin staining, irregular shallow border — textbook venous.

failed_4wk_swc.evidence: More than 4 weeks of compression with <50% area reduction documented across serial measurements.

dx_over_3mo.evidence: Venous ulcer documented since 03/02/2026 (~14 weeks, > 3 months).

cases.teaching_moment: Opal's chart is a strong venous workup — reflux confirmed, CEAP C6/VCSS 12, 14 weeks documented, a real 4-week standard-care failure including compliance with compression therapy, clean qualifying wound. She clears every CTP gate but one: there's no ABI, toe pressure, or even a pedal-pulse exam in the record. CMS requires documented adequate perfusion before a skin substitute — ABI no less than 0.60, or toe pressure over 30 mmHg. Prior to the application of a CTP an ABI or toe pressure to clear the patient for the CTP application must be obtained and documented in her record. Without it the CTP claim is denied on review — and clinically you may be compressing (and about to graft) a limb that could be mixed disease, which can drive an ischemic injury. The diagnosis was never the problem. The missing diagnostics for appropriate vascular insufficiency vs mixed disease.
cases.difficulty_explanation: Diagnosis is right and the chart looks thorough — reflux study, CEAP/VCSS, documented failure, clean qualifying wound. The missing diagnostics is the ABI or toe pressure which could negatively impact the patient's clinical condition as well as reimbursement for a CTP.

patient.name: Royce Tatum
dx: Traumatic open wound, anterior left lower leg, with exposed tibia
Status post motorcycle collision (11 weeks prior)

radiology.finding: No marrow signal abnormality; negative for osteomyelitis

patient.wound_dressing: Saline-moistened gauze, daily
patient.clinical_notes: 58-year-old male, 11 weeks status post motorcycle collision with an open anterior left lower-leg wound. Exam: wound bed over the anterior tibia with granulation tissue present; probe-to-bone positive with exposed cortical bone visible at the base; scant serous exudate, no necrosis. At the 06/08 visit, new periwound erythema and edema were noted and could indicate potential infection. Serial measurements show the wound still slowly closing, though the rate of reduction has slowed at the most recent visit. MRI of the left tibia negative for osteomyelitis; ESR and CRP within normal limits. After 4 weeks of standard of care the plan is to apply a cellular/tissue product (skin substitute) to accelerate closure; continue daily dressing changes.

bone_exposure_documented.evidence: Probe-to-bone positive; exposed cortical bone visible at base.

wound_characteristics.evidence: Anterior left lower leg; serial measurements; granulating base, scant exudate.

osteo_evaluation.evidence: MRI negative for osteomyelitis; ESR/CRP WNL.

infection_addressed.evidence: New periwound erythema and edema at the 06/08 visit, with a decelerating healing trend = signs of local wound infection, not addressed before the CTP plan. L36690 requires a clean, infection-free bed; a CTP over an infected wound is not supportable until the infection is treated and the bed re-confirmed clean. The negative osteo MRI and normal ESR/CRP rule out deep/bone infection — they do not clear the surface.

cases.teaching_moment: Royce's chart looks CTP-ready at a glance: exposed tibia documented, osteomyelitis ruled out by MRI, ESR/CRP normal, and a wound still measuring smaller every visit. That positive trend is the trap. Look again at the 06/08 exam — new periwound erythema and edema, and a healing rate that is slowing, not holding. Those are signs of a local wound infection taking hold. The lesson: ruling out osteomyelitis is not the same as confirming a clean wound. A negative MRI and normal ESR/CRP tell you the bone is fine; they say nothing about the surface. Medicare requires the wound be clean and free of infection before a skin substitute goes on, so a CTP over this bed is not supportable until the infection is treated and the bed re-confirmed clean. Catch the erythema and edema against the reassuring measurements and you catch the denial. And once it is clean: a CTP over exposed bone still needs a product whose package label approves exposed-bone use — but that is the next gate, not this one.
cases.difficulty_explanation: Everything on the front of the chart says go: exposed bone documented, osteo cleanly ruled out, wound shrinking. The miss is subtle — new periwound erythema and edema and a decelerating trend that mean the bed is infected, not clean. Read the diagnosis and trend and you pass it; audit whether the wound actually meets the clean, infection-free bar a CTP requires, and you catch the denial.

patient.name: Hollis Crabtree
dx: Chronic peripheral neuropathy secondary to long-standing alcohol use
Non-healing neuropathic ulcer, right plantar first metatarsal head

radiology.finding: Cortical irregularity and lytic change at the first metatarsal head, concerning for osteomyelitis; recommend further workup

patient.wound_dressing: Off-loaded with removable CAM boot; foam dressing changed three times weekly
patient.clinical_notes: 64-year-old male with chronic alcohol-related peripheral neuropathy, seen for a non-healing right plantar first metatarsal head ulcer first documented 03/16/2026 (~12 weeks). No history of diabetes mellitus — HbA1c 5.4%, fasting glucose normal. Protective sensation absent at multiple plantar sites on Semmes-Weinstein 10 g monofilament; vibratory sense diminished. Pedal pulses 2+ palpable; ABI 0.95 bilaterally — adequate perfusion, no arterial component. Ulcer over the first metatarsal head with a round, punched-out border and callused rim; base granular but probes to bone. Off-loaded with a removable CAM boot since 03/23; patient compliant with off-loading and dressing changes. Over more than 4 weeks of conservative care the wound shows less than 50% (<50%) area reduction. Plain film 05/20 shows cortical irregularity and lytic change at the first metatarsal head concerning for osteomyelitis; no MRI, bone biopsy, ESR/CRP, or infectious-disease consult is on file, and osteomyelitis has not been excluded. Plan: team queuing a cellular/tissue product (skin substitute) application at the next visit.

neuropathy_documented.evidence: Chronic alcohol-related peripheral neuropathy documented, with the underlying cause named (alcohol, not diabetes).

protective_sensation_testing.evidence: Protective sensation absent at multiple plantar sites on Semmes-Weinstein 10 g monofilament.

location_weightbearing.evidence: Wound over the right plantar first metatarsal head — a weight-bearing pressure point.

offloading_documented.evidence: Off-loaded with a removable CAM boot since 03/23.

diabetes_status.evidence: Diabetes status documented and negative (HbA1c 5.4%, no history of diabetes) — correctly stays Neuropathic, not reclassified to DFU.

perfusion_adequate.evidence: ABI 0.95 with 2+ palpable pedal pulses — adequate perfusion (≥0.60), rules out an arterial/neuroischemic component.

failed_4wk_swc.evidence: More than 4 weeks of conservative care with <50% area reduction; patient compliance documented.

osteo_infection_excluded.evidence: Ulcer probes to bone and the 05/20 plain film shows lytic change concerning for osteomyelitis — yet no MRI, bone biopsy, ESR/CRP, or ID consult is on file. Osteomyelitis has NOT been excluded, and L36690 bars a CTP graft over underlying osteomyelitis or a nidus of infection.

standard_wound_therapy_documented.evidence: N/A — this is a CTP claim, not an NPWT claim, so the NPWT standard-therapy / weekly-measurement gate is not the operative standard here.

cases.teaching_moment: Hollis's cause is documented (alcohol, not diabetes → stays Neuropathic), monofilament loss, weight-bearing location, offloading, adequate perfusion (ABI 0.95 rules out arterial), a real compliant 4-week failure. But the ulcer probes to bone and the film shows lytic change concerning for osteomyelitis — and osteo was never excluded. Medicare bars a CTP graft over underlying osteomyelitis or a nidus of infection. Graft over unaddressed osteo and you're not just facing a denial — you're sealing a skin substitute over an active bone infection. Another issue to consider is that the patient’s record does not have an ICD-10 code documented that reflects the underlying mechanism of the neuropathy.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The etiology is right (non-diabetic neuropathic, correctly not reclassified to DFU) and the chart looks thorough: documented cause, monofilament, off-loading, ABI, a compliant 4-week failure. The catch is a single criterion — the CTP-disqualifying osteomyelitis concern (probe-to-bone plus a lytic film) was never excluded. Read for what is present and you pass it; audit against Medicare’s 'no underlying osteo or nidus of infection' gate and you catch it. The NPWT standard-therapy criterion is N/A here because this is a CTP claim, not NPWT — a clean example of when N/A is the correct answer.

patient.name: Wanda Sturgill
dx: Chronic non-healing ulcer, left distal lateral malleolus
Peripheral arterial disease / lower-extremity arterial disease (LEAD)

radiology.finding: Right ABI 1.65, Left ABI 1.59

patient.wound_dressing: Local wound care with non-adherent foam; no compression applied given arterial disease
patient.clinical_notes: 53-year-old female with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 16%), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and known peripheral arterial disease, seen for a chronic non-healing ulcer of the left distal lateral malleolus, first documented 04/06/2026 and slowly enlarging despite local wound care. She previously received prior daily wound care through a home-health service. Exam: well-defined, punched-out wound border with a pale, dusky base and minimal exudate; the wound is painful, worse with elevation. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are faint to non-palpable bilaterally. No signs of cellulitis or infection. Former smoker; tobacco cessation reinforced. ABI obtained 05/18/2026: Right 1.65, Left 1.59 — documented in the chart as 'within normal limits, perfusion adequate.' No toe pressures (TBI), arterial duplex, or angiography are on file, and no vascular-surgery referral has been placed. Compression has not been applied given the arterial picture. Plan: optimize the wound bed and advance to a cellular/tissue product (skin substitute) at the next visit, treating perfusion as adequate per the ABI.

arterial_perfusion_documented.evidence: The only perfusion data is an ABI of 1.65/1.59. An ABI >1.3 indicates non-compressible, calcified vessels (classic in long-standing diabetes) and is uninterpretable — the criterion itself says to use TBI/toe pressure when ABI >1.3. No TBI, toe pressure, duplex, or angiogram is on file, and faint/absent distal pulses point to real ischemia. Adequate perfusion is NOT validly documented; charting the calcified ABI as 'perfusion adequate' is the trap.

wound_characteristics_arterial.evidence: Well-defined punched-out border, pale dusky base, painful, distal location — textbook arterial morphology.

compression_avoided.evidence: No compression applied given the arterial picture — appropriately withheld.

vascular_referral.evidence: Severe arterial disease (faint/absent distal pulses, an uninterpretable ABI masking true ischemia) — vascular evaluation/revascularization is clearly indicated, yet no vascular-surgery referral is documented. The falsely-high ABI made referral look unnecessary; it isn't.

history_prior_treatment.evidence: Prior daily wound care through a home-health service documented; current wound onset 04/06/2026 with serial follow-up.

tobacco_status.evidence: Former smoker; tobacco cessation reinforced (primary LEAD risk factor).

infection_addressed.evidence: Infection assessed — no signs of cellulitis or infection.

cases.teaching_moment: Wanda's chart looks ready to graft — with the exception of a HbA1c of 16% indicates that the patient’s diabetic is not under control in addition an ABI of 1.65/1.59 charted as "perfusion adequate." That ABI is a mirage: >1.3 means calcified, non-compressible vessels (common in long-standing diabetes), so the number is uninterpretable, not reassuring. The real signals say arterial — faint/absent distal pulses, a punched-out painful enlarging distal ulcer, known PAD. No toe pressure, duplex, or angiogram was obtained, and no vascular referral was placed. Take the ABI at face value and you clear the perfusion gate, graft a critically ischemic limb, and the graft fails — or worse. The kill-shot: a high ABI in a diabetic is a red flag, not a green light. Confirm with TBI/toe pressure when ABI >1.3, and refer. Two criteria fail, both from the same misread.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The chart is framed as a diabetic wound with 'adequate perfusion per ABI,' and the reassuring 1.6 ABI tempts you to clear perfusion and advance to a graft. The correct call is an arterial ulcer with perfusion that was never validly established: ABI >1.3 = calcified/uninterpretable, no TBI or duplex, faint distal pulses, no vascular referral. One misread (trusting a calcified ABI) cascades into two failed criteria (perfusion not documented + referral not made).

patient.name: Dale Hutchins
dx: Venous stasis ulcer, left medial lower leg
Chronic venous insufficiency, bilateral lower extremities

radiology.study: Venous duplex ultrasound, left lower extremity
radiology.finding: Great saphenous reflux 2.1 s; deep system patent, no DVT
Left ABI 0.52, Right ABI 0.58

patient.wound_dressing: Full multilayer compression wrap (Profore), changed weekly; foam primary dressing
patient.clinical_notes: 68-year-old male carried as a venous stasis ulcer of the left medial lower leg, first documented 03/24/2026. Venous duplex 03/30 confirmed great saphenous reflux, and the leg shows hemosiderin staining, varicosities, and 1+ edema — a venous-appearing picture. However, the wound base also shows patchy pale and necrotic areas, the border is irregular, and the patient reports the leg pain has worsened since compression was started, worse with elevation. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are diminished bilaterally. ABI obtained 04/13: left 0.52, right 0.58. Despite the low ABI, the plan has continued standard full multilayer compression (Profore) weekly, treating the ulcer as purely venous. Over more than 8 weeks of compression therapy the wound shows less than 50% area reduction and is mildly enlarging. No vascular-surgery referral has been placed and compression has not been reduced or withheld. Plan: continue weekly compression.

arterial_component_documented.evidence: ABI 0.52 (left) / 0.58 (right) with diminished distal pulses documents reduced perfusion — a real arterial component.

venous_component_documented.evidence: Great saphenous reflux on duplex plus hemosiderin staining and varicosities — a real venous component.

compression_modified_for_arterial.evidence: Full multilayer compression (Profore) was applied and continued despite an ABI of 0.52 — compression is CONTRAINDICATED below 0.6 and must be reduced or withheld, not run at full strength. Worsening pain since compression started is an ischemic red flag. This is the harm: full compression on a critically arterial limb.

vascular_referral.evidence: ABI 0.52 with diminished pulses warrants vascular evaluation/referral, but none is documented — the venous label meant the arterial component was never worked up.

wound_characteristics_mixed.evidence: Lower-leg wound with mixed picture — granulation alongside patchy pale/necrotic areas and an irregular border — consistent with mixed arterial-venous, not pure venous.

failed_4wk_swc.evidence: More than 8 weeks of compression therapy with <50% area reduction (mildly enlarging) — failure of standard therapy with the specific intervention cited.

cases.teaching_moment: Dale's chart is carried as venous, and it has reason to be — reflux, hemosiderin, varicosities — so full compression went on and stayed on. But an ABI of 0.52 is sitting in the same chart, and compression is contraindicated below 0.6. This isn't pure venous; it's mixed, and the arterial component makes standard full compression dangerous. The tells are there: diminished pulses and pain that got worse once compression started and leg elevation indicates ischemia. Anchor on the venous features and you keep wrapping a critically under-perfused leg, drive ischemic injury, and never refer to vascular. The kill-shot: check the ABI before you trust the venous label — a low ABI flips the etiology to mixed and flips compression from treatment to harm.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The front-page diagnosis (venous stasis ulcer) is half right, and the venous findings are real, so the venous label and full compression feel justified. The correct call is MIXED arterial-venous: an ABI of 0.52 in the same chart makes full compression contraindicated, diminished pulses, and compression-worsened pain confirm the arterial half. Trust the venous label and you pass it (and harm the patient); check the ABI before compressing and you catch it.

patient.name: Cecil Roark
dx: Bilateral neuropathic diabetic foot ulcers, metatarsophalangeal soles, ~10 years
Sensory, motor, and autonomic peripheral neuropathy
Moderate chronic arterial ischemia (neuro-ischemic), with venous hypertension left leg

radiology.study: Arterial Doppler ultrasound, bilateral lower extremities
radiology.finding: Calcified atherosclerotic plaques in distal territories with biphasic flow; moderate chronic arterial ischemia
Right 1.2, Left 1.3 — non-diagnostic given vessel calcification
No marrow edema or cortical destruction; negative for osteomyelitis in either foot

patient.wound_dressing: Calcium alginate to control exudate; offloading with a 1.5 cm pad and a walking stick
patient.clinical_notes: 61-year-old male with type 2 diabetes mellitus of 14 years, on insulin, with established sensory, motor, and autonomic peripheral neuropathy. He has carried bilateral neuropathic foot ulcers in the metatarsophalangeal sole regions for ten years, never fully healing, with multiple prior hospitalizations for recurrent infection requiring debridement and IV antibiotics; he has repeatedly declined amputation. HbA1c is 7.4% and well managed on insulin; BMI 24. Exam: sole ulcers, right 2x3 cm and left 4x3 cm, with heavy hyperkeratosis, swollen exudative borders, malodor, and macerated interdigital spaces; onychomycosis of all nails. The probe-to-bone test is negative, and MRI of both feet is negative for osteomyelitis (no marrow edema or cortical destruction). There is moderate Charcot arthropathy of the left foot, not separately addressed in the current plan. Vascular: dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are weak on the right and absent on the left; the patient reports intermittent claudication at under 150 meters and nighttime rest pain relieved by dependency. Doppler ultrasound shows calcified atherosclerotic plaques with biphasic flow consistent with moderate chronic arterial ischemia; ABI is 1.2 right and 1.3 left and is non-diagnostic given the calcification. A vascular-surgery referral has been placed for possible revascularization. Offloading is documented with a 1.5 cm pad and a walking stick, but the patient's offloading compliance has been poor and inconsistent. No Wagner grade is assigned in the record, and no nutritional assessment (albumin or prealbumin) is documented. Wound culture grew Staphylococcus aureus; the plan includes antimicrobial therapy and continued debridement. Plan: continue local wound care, reinforce offloading, await vascular evaluation.

diabetes_documented.evidence: Type 2 diabetes of 14 years, insulin-treated — type and control documented.

wagner_grade.evidence: No Wagner grade is assigned anywhere in the record. Without it, depth/severity and the CTP/HBOT eligibility tier can't be established.

vascular_assessment.evidence: Perfusion was assessed correctly: weak/absent pulses, claudication and rest pain, Doppler showing calcified plaques with biphasic flow, the ABI explicitly flagged as non-diagnostic due to calcification, and a vascular referral placed. The calcified ABI was recognized, not trusted.

offloading_documented.evidence: Offloading documented — a 1.5 cm pad and a walking stick.

offloading_compliance.evidence: An offloading device is documented, but the record explicitly notes poor, inconsistent compliance. If the patient isn't actually offloading, the standard/conservative-care requirement isn't truly met.

failed_4wk_swc.evidence: Ten years of non-healing despite repeated standard care — well beyond the 4-week threshold with <50% reduction. Osteomyelitis is excluded by MRI of both feet (negative), not by the probe-to-bone alone — appropriate given the chronicity, prior osteo history, and active infection.

charcot_ruled_out.evidence: Moderate Charcot arthropathy of the left foot is present and not separately addressed or staged (acute vs inactive) — an unaddressed complicating diagnosis that changes offloading and healing expectations.

nutritional_assessment.evidence: BMI is noted but no nutritional assessment (albumin/prealbumin) is documented — a host-factor optimization gap in a chronic non-healing DFU.

infection_addressed.evidence: Wound culture obtained (Staphylococcus aureus) with antimicrobial therapy and debridement in the plan; osteomyelitis excluded by MRI (negative).

cases.teaching_moment: Cecil's DFU looks well worked up, and in important ways it is: the diabetes and glucose are controlled and documented, and the vascular workup is exemplary — they recognized the ABI was calcified and non-diagnostic, used Doppler, and referred to vascular — and osteomyelitis was excluded the right way, by MRI rather than a probe-to-bone alone — which is exactly the opposite of trusting a misleading number. But the claim is swiss-cheese. Four independent documentation gaps each sink it on their own: no Wagner grade (severity tier can't be established), explicitly poor offloading compliance (the conservative-care requirement isn't really being met), an unaddressed moderate Charcot arthropathy (a complicating diagnosis that changes offloading and prognosis), and no nutritional assessment (host-factor optimization undocumented). There's no single fatal hole — there are four small ones the claim falls through. The lesson: a DFU claim isn't diagnosis plus perfusion; it's a stack of severity, offloading, complicating-condition, and host-factor requirements, and the auditor reads every layer — not just the strong ones.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The etiology is right and the headline items look strong (controlled, documented diabetes and an exemplary vascular workup that correctly distrusts a calcified ABI), which tempts you to pass it. It still fails, because four separate coverage requirements are each unmet: Wagner grade, offloading compliance, Charcot addressed, and nutritional assessment. No single kill-shot — it's swiss-cheese, and you only catch it by auditing every criterion instead of stopping at the strong ones.

patient.name: Marlene Dyer
dx: Diabetic foot ulcer, right plantar first metatarsal head
Diabetic peripheral neuropathy with loss of protective sensation

radiology.finding: No osteomyelitis; no Charcot changes; no fracture or joint disorganization

radiology.study: ABI / Toe-Brachial Index, right lower extremity
radiology.finding: ABI 1.02, TBI 0.78 — adequate perfusion, vessels non-calcified

patient.wound_dressing: Moisture-balanced foam; offloading with a total contact cast (TCC)
patient.clinical_notes: 59-year-old female with well-controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.2%) and documented peripheral neuropathy, seen for a plantar diabetic foot ulcer over the right first metatarsal head, first documented 04/20/2026. Loss of protective sensation confirmed on Semmes-Weinstein 10 g monofilament. The wound is full-thickness with a clean granular base and no exposed bone; probe-to-bone is negative and it is documented as Wagner Grade 2. No clinical signs of infection. Vascular: dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable; ABI 1.02 with TBI 0.78 — adequate perfusion with non-calcified vessels. Foot radiographs are negative for Charcot changes, and acute Charcot is ruled out. Offloading is provided with a total contact cast (TCC), and the patient is documented as compliant with the cast and non-weight-bearing. Nutrition: albumin 3.8 g/dL and prealbumin within normal limits, with a dietitian consult on file. Over more than 6 weeks of standard wound care (offloading, debridement, moisture-balanced dressings) the wound shows less than 50% area reduction, with documented patient compliance. Plan: advance to a cellular/tissue product (skin substitute) at the next visit.

diabetes_documented.evidence: Type 2 diabetes, well-controlled, type and management documented (metformin + empagliflozin).

wagner_grade.evidence: Documented as Wagner Grade 2 — full-thickness without exposed bone, abscess, or osteomyelitis (probe-to-bone negative).

vascular_assessment.evidence: ABI 1.02 with a confirming TBI 0.78 and palpable pulses — adequate perfusion, vessels non-calcified.

offloading_documented.evidence: Offloading provided with a total contact cast (TCC).

offloading_compliance.evidence: Patient documented as compliant with the cast and non-weight-bearing.

failed_4wk_swc.evidence: More than 6 weeks of documented standard wound care with <50% area reduction; osteomyelitis ruled out (probe-to-bone negative, radiograph negative).

charcot_ruled_out.evidence: Foot radiographs negative for Charcot changes; acute Charcot ruled out.

nutritional_assessment.evidence: Albumin 3.8 g/dL and prealbumin within normal limits, with a dietitian consult on file.

infection_addressed.evidence: Assessed — no clinical signs of infection; probe-to-bone negative rules out osteomyelitis.

cases.teaching_moment: Marlene is what a clean, fully-supported diabetic foot ulcer claim looks like — the calibration baseline. Walk every criterion and each one is met and documented: diabetes type and control, a documented Wagner grade, adequate perfusion confirmed the right way (a normal ABI BACKED by a TBI, non-calcified vessels — no mirage), offloading with a total contact cast AND documented compliance, controlled glucose, a real >4-week standard-care failure, Charcot actively ruled out on radiograph, a nutritional assessment with labs, and infection assessed with osteomyelitis ruled out. Nothing to catch — and that's the point.
cases.difficulty_explanation: A clean qualifier with no trap. Every DIABETIC_ULCER criterion is documented and satisfied, including the ones that bite in harder cases (perfusion confirmed with a TBI rather than a bare ABI, offloading plus compliance, Charcot ruled out, nutrition assessed). The teaching value is calibration: this is the 'what good looks like' anchor that makes the gaps in every other case legible.

patient.name: Bernice Stallard
dx: Stage IV pressure injury, left gluteal region over the ischial tuberosity
Quadriplegia following meningitis, fully dependent in ADLs
patient.wound_dressing: Foam with enzymatic debridement; daily pH-balanced cleansing
patient.clinical_notes: 54-year-old woman with quadriplegia following meningitis, fully dependent in activities of daily living, who developed a pressure injury of the left gluteal region over the ischial tuberosity during prolonged immobility and bed rest. The injury progressed to NPUAP Stage IV with an undermining pocket; NPIAP scoring is documented and trended weekly (peak score 45). Pressure and shear from immobility are the confirmed etiology. Comorbidities: type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.4%) and hypertension; Braden Scale 12. Management: a low-air-loss air mattress and chair cushion for pressure redistribution, a scheduled q2-hour repositioning protocol, enzymatic debridement of necrotic tissue, and daily pH-balanced wound cleansing. Nutrition: dietitian consult on file with albumin 3.4 g/dL and protein supplementation initiated. The record does not document any moisture or incontinence management plan (barrier protection, an incontinence schedule, or containment products) despite the gluteal location and the patient's dependent, immobile status. Plan: continue support surface, repositioning, debridement, and local wound care.

stage_documented.evidence: NPUAP Stage IV documented with weekly NPIAP scoring.

location_bony_prominence.evidence: Left gluteal region over the ischial tuberosity — a bony prominence / pressure point.

pressure_etiology.evidence: Pressure and shear from quadriplegia and prolonged immobility are the confirmed etiology.

support_surface.evidence: Low-air-loss air mattress and chair cushion for pressure redistribution .

repositioning.evidence: Scheduled q2-hour repositioning protocol documented (Stage IV on the pelvis).

moisture_incontinence_managed.evidence: No moisture or incontinence management plan is documented (no barrier protection, incontinence schedule, or containment products) despite a sacral/gluteal Stage IV wound in a dependent, immobile patient — a real healing-impairment and recurrence-risk gap, and the spot where pressure and moisture damage blur.

nutritional_assessment.evidence: Dietitian consult on file with albumin 3.4 g/dL and protein supplementation initiated.

cases.teaching_moment: Bernice's Stage IV PI is a model claim by most measures — staged and trended (NPIAP), a clear bony prominence, pressure/shear etiology incorrectly distinguished from moisture-associated skin damage, a real support surface, a scheduled repositioning protocol, and a nutritional assessment with labs. One element is simply missing: no moisture or incontinence management plan anywhere. On a gluteal wound in a dependent, immobile, likely-incontinent patient, unmanaged moisture impairs healing, drives recurrence, and is exactly where pressure injury and moisture-associated skin damage start to blur.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The etiology is right and the chart looks complete: staging with NPIAP, bony-prominence location, confirmed pressure etiology, support surface, repositioning, and a nutritional assessment. The catch is a single absent element — moisture/incontinence management — which matters most precisely because of the gluteal location and the patient's incontinence risk.

patient.name: Harlan Tipton
dx: Non-healing wound with exposed bone, right mandible (referred for wound management)
History of oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, status post chemoradiation completed ~15 months prior (~66 Gy to the right neck/mandible field)

radiology.finding: Cortical disruption and a small bony sequestrum at the right mandibular body within the prior radiation field; no drainable abscess; findings consistent with osteoradionecrosis rather than primary osteomyelitis

patient.wound_dressing: Intraoral saline rinses; small external gauze to draining orocutaneous tract, changed daily
patient.clinical_notes: 68-year-old male referred to the outpatient wound care clinic for a non-healing wound with exposed bone at the right mandible. History of right oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma treated with chemoradiation (~66 Gy to the right neck/mandible field), completed roughly 15 months ago. The lesion began after a post-radiation lower-right molar extraction and has failed to heal over ~4 months. Exam: exposed, dull necrotic cortical bone visible at the right mandibular body intraorally, with a small draining orocutaneous tract at the right jawline; surrounding mucosa is atrophic and radiation-changed; trismus limits opening to ~25 mm; foul odor; pain 6/10. No fluctuant abscess, no spreading cellulitis, no systemic sepsis. CT consistent with osteoradionecrosis (irradiated, hypovascular bone with sequestrum), not primary osteomyelitis. Wound essentially static over serial visits despite local care. Plan as written: enroll in outpatient wound care; debride necrotic bone at bedside and begin negative-pressure wound therapy, with skin-substitute application considered if it fails to progress.

cases.teaching_moment: Harlan's chart has exposed bone, a static non-healing wound, and a probe-able necrotic surface — which pulls you straight toward an Exposed-Bone call and an NPWT order. Stop at the history. This bone sits inside a ~66 Gy radiation field, and the CT reads osteoradionecrosis, not osteomyelitis. Irradiated bone is hypoxic, hypovascular, and hypocellular — it cannot heal on the standard wound-care or NPWT pathway, and bedside debridement of radionecrotic mandible without addressing the radiation injury can extend the necrosis. Osteoradionecrosis of the mandible is a recognized HBOT indication and an oral-maxillofacial/ENT problem; it bypasses the outpatient wound-care front door entirely. The correct call is Not a WC Pathway — refer to HBOT and OMFS/ENT. Running NPWT, CTP, or debridement claims through the outpatient WC clinic here is a wrong-pathway denial and, worse, delays the one therapy that actually addresses the irradiated tissue.
cases.difficulty_explanation: Every surface cue (exposed bone, non-healing, necrotic base) screams a wound-care etiology, specifically Exposed Bone → NPWT. The radiation history is the whole case: it reroutes the claim out of the outpatient WC pathway to HBOT-direct. You don't grade this wound — you recognize it isn't yours to claim. The curveball is that the most 'gradeable-looking' finding (exposed bone) is exactly the bait.

patient.name: Lonnie Frasure
dx: Chronic non-healing ulcer, left posterior calf, arising within an old burn-scar contracture
History of full-thickness flame burn to the left lower leg ~32 years prior, healed with dense scarring

radiology.study: Arterial ABI / pulse exam, left lower extremity
radiology.finding: ABI 0.96; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable — perfusion adequate, no arterial component

patient.wound_dressing: Sharp debridement at intervals; foam + antimicrobial dressing, changed 3x/week
patient.clinical_notes: 72-year-old male with a chronic ulcer of the left posterior calf, sitting within a dense burn-scar contracture from a flame burn ~32 years ago. The wound has been managed as a chronic lower-leg ulcer for ~8 months with appropriate standard care — serial sharp debridement, moist/antimicrobial dressings, and adequate perfusion confirmed (ABI 0.96, palpable pulses). Despite consistent appropriate therapy the wound has not improved; it is slowly enlarging across serial measurements. Exam: rolled, everted, indurated wound margins with exophytic heaped-up friable tissue at the base that bleeds easily on contact; persistent serosanguinous exudate and foul odor without surrounding cellulitis or systemic signs of infection. No venous duplex/reflux study on file and no clinical venous stigmata (no varicosities, hemosiderin, or lipodermatosclerosis documented); no diabetes; perfusion adequate. No wound biopsy has ever been obtained. Plan as written: continue debridement and dressings; advance to a skin substitute (CTP) this visit to push closure.

cases.teaching_moment: Lonnie's wound invites you to pick an etiology and grade it — but every classic determination fails here, and the morphology is shouting the reason. It is not arterial (ABI 0.96, pulses present) and there is nothing on file to call it venous (no reflux study, no venous stigmata), so the workup cannot support any etiology determination yet. More important, the wound has the textbook red flags of malignant transformation: a chronic non-healing ulcer of ~8 months that has failed appropriate therapy and is enlarging, sitting in a decades-old burn scar, with rolled everted indurated margins and exophytic friable tissue that bleeds easily. That is the picture of a Marjolin's ulcer — an aggressive squamous cell carcinoma arising in chronic scar/wound — and it has never been biopsied. The correct call is Need More Information: biopsy before you name it. Advancing to a skin substitute over a possible cancer is both an unsupportable claim and a serious clinical harm — it grafts over and delays the diagnosis of a malignancy. No etiology, no advanced-therapy claim, until the path comes back.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The chart reads like a gradeable chronic ulcer and the plan (advance to CTP) looks like ordinary escalation, which is the bait. The L5 move is recognizing what's missing and what's atypical at the same time: the classifying workup can't support any etiology, and the rolled/everted/exophytic morphology in an old burn scar is a biopsy trigger for Marjolin's. You are not choosing an etiology — you are recognizing you can't, yet, and that grafting now would be the real error.

patient.name: Boyd Sizemore
dx: Chronic wound with exposed bone, anterior left leg (referred for advanced wound therapy)
Chronic osteomyelitis, left tibia (Cierny-Mader type IV, diffuse)
Non-union, distal third left tibia, status post Gustilo IIIA open fracture ~1 year prior with prior external fixation
medications: Recently completed an outside course of oral antibiotics

radiology.finding: Non-union of the distal third tibia with sequestrum and involucrum and lucency (osteolysis) around prior pin tracts — features of chronic osteomyelitis
Normal vascularity, no stenosis — perfusion adequate, no arterial component

patient.wound_dressing: Saline-moistened gauze to exposed bone, daily; gauze packing of draining tract
patient.clinical_notes: 45-year-old male referred to the outpatient wound care clinic for a chronic non-healing wound with exposed bone at the anterior left leg, ~8 x 3 cm, with purulent discharge and previously infected external-fixator pin sites. One year ago he sustained a Gustilo IIIA open comminuted distal-third left tibia fracture, treated elsewhere with external fixation; the course was complicated by deep infection requiring multiple wound debridements and a prolonged course of culture-directed antibiotics, and below-knee amputation was offered for refractory infection, which he declined. Bone culture grew MRSA. Plain films show non-union with sequestrum and involucrum and osteolysis around the old pin tracts — chronic osteomyelitis, left tibia. CT angiography shows normal vascularity (no arterial component). Labs: WBC 13.3 (elevated); CRP within normal limits — markers can run quiet in chronic osteomyelitis, so the films and bone culture carry the diagnosis. Exam: exposed, dull cortical tibial bone at the base, probe-to-bone positive, surrounding granulation with foul purulent exudate; wound essentially static / mildly enlarging over serial visits despite local care. Plan as written: begin negative-pressure wound therapy to the exposed-bone wound and consider a skin substitute (CTP) to accelerate closure.

prior_osteo_same_location.evidence: Chronic osteomyelitis of the left tibia documented at the same site as the wound, following the prior open fracture and infected fixation.

confirming_studies.evidence: Plain films show sequestrum and involucrum with pin-tract osteolysis; bone culture grew MRSA — radiographic + microbiologic confirmation.

antibiotics_or_surgery.evidence: Multiple prior wound debridements and a prolonged course of culture-directed antibiotics documented.

refractory_documented.evidence: Infection refractory to prior medical and surgical management — amputation was offered for the refractory course and declined.

cases.teaching_moment: Boyd's wound has exposed tibial bone and a team eyeing NPWT and a skin substitute — which pulls you straight toward an Exposed-Bone call. Read the bone instead. Sequestrum and involucrum on film, MRSA on bone culture, a non-union after a Gustilo IIIA open fracture, multiple prior debridements and prolonged antibiotics, and an amputation already offered for refractory infection: this is active, refractory chronic osteomyelitis. That is the etiology — not 'a wound that happens to expose bone' — and the distinction is the whole claim. Untreated/active osteomyelitis is a hard contraindication to NPWT, and exposed bone is an explicit CTP exclusion, so both outpatient advanced therapies are off the table. This wound needs surgical debridement, ID-directed antibiotics, and reconstruction — with HBOT considered for refractory osteomyelitis — not an outpatient NPWT or skin-substitute claim. Note too that the inflammatory markers run quiet (normal CRP); in chronic osteomyelitis the films and the bone culture, not the labs, carry the diagnosis.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The exposed bone is the bait: it pulls toward an Exposed-Bone call and an NPWT/CTP order that both look like ordinary wound care. The bone findings — sequestrum, involucrum, MRSA on bone culture, a refractory course — name the real etiology as chronic osteomyelitis, and that diagnosis is exactly what makes NPWT contraindicated and CTP excluded. Pick the etiology off the surface finding and you misclassify and green-light a non-covered, contraindicated therapy; read the bone and you catch it.

patient.name: Wendell Combs
dx: Acute osteomyelitis, left third metatarsal (contiguous, post-puncture)
Puncture wound, plantar left forefoot, ~12 days prior
medications: IV cefazolin (culture-directed antibiotic therapy), per ID

radiology.study: MRI left foot with and without contrast
radiology.finding: Marrow edema and enhancement of the third metatarsal with adjacent soft-tissue inflammation, consistent with acute osteomyelitis; no sequestrum, involucrum, or chronic changes

patient.wound_dressing: Daily saline-moistened gauze to the puncture tract after debridement of the entry site
patient.clinical_notes: 56-year-old male, non-diabetic (HbA1c 5.5%), seen for a plantar left forefoot puncture wound sustained ~12 days ago (stepped on debris through a work boot). Over the past week he developed worsening localized pain with erythema, warmth, tenderness, and edema over the dorsal midfoot, plus a low-grade fever. No prior wound or bone infection at this site. Labs: WBC 14.8 (elevated); ESR and CRP both elevated. MRI of the left foot shows marrow edema and enhancement of the third metatarsal with adjacent soft-tissue inflammation, consistent with acute osteomyelitis, with no sequestrum, involucrum, or chronic features (distinguishing acute from chronic disease). A bone aspirate culture was obtained and grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). The patient was started on IV cefazolin as culture-directed antibiotic therapy with infectious-disease co-management. Perfusion intact (palpable pedal pulses, ABI 1.04). Plan: sharp debridement of devitalized tissue at the puncture tract (covered wound-care procedure), continue culture-directed IV cefazolin with infectious-disease co-management, and serial monitoring of inflammatory markers; the wound is not a candidate for a cellular/tissue product (active osteomyelitis contraindicates it) or for hyperbaric oxygen (reserved for chronic refractory osteomyelitis, not acute).

confirming_studies.evidence: MRI shows marrow edema and enhancement of the third metatarsal consistent with acute osteomyelitis (no chronic features); supported by elevated WBC/ESR/CRP.

infection_signs.evidence: Erythema, warmth, tenderness, and edema over the affected foot with low-grade fever documented.

culture_documented.evidence: Bone aspirate culture obtained and grew MSSA, establishing the organism and sensitivities.

antibiotics_documented.evidence: IV cefazolin started as culture-directed antibiotic therapy with ID co-management.

therapy_pathway_appropriate.evidence: The plan documents the covered wound-care pathway — sharp debridement of devitalized tissue plus culture-directed antibiotics and infectious-disease co-management — and correctly withholds the advanced therapies: a CTP is contraindicated by the active osteomyelitis, and HBOT is reserved for chronic refractory osteo, not acute. Right covered move, escalations correctly avoided.

cases.teaching_moment: Wendell is the calibration anchor for acute osteomyelitis — a clean, fully supported determination, so there's nothing to catch, and that's the point. The picture is unmistakably acute, not chronic: a recent puncture wound, about twelve days of evolving symptoms, and an MRI showing marrow edema and enhancement with no sequestrum or involucrum — the chronic findings are deliberately absent. Every documentation element is present: a confirming study (MRI, backed by elevated WBC/ESR/CRP), documented local infection signs (erythema, warmth, tenderness, edema), a bone aspirate culture that named the organism (MSSA) before committing to therapy, and culture-directed antibiotics with ID co-management. That ordering — confirm, culture, then treat to the organism — is exactly what a defensible acute-osteo record looks like. When you see this chart, the correct read is simply: acute osteomyelitis, properly worked up and documented. And the pathway matches — the covered move is debridement of the devitalized tissue alongside culture-directed antibiotics and ID, with the advanced therapies correctly left on the shelf: a skin substitute is contraindicated over active osteomyelitis, and HBOT is reserved for chronic refractory disease, not acute. That is the line that separates Wendell from the chronic picture — same bone-infection family, different covered pathway.
cases.difficulty_explanation: A clean, fully documented acute osteomyelitis with every criterion met: confirming MRI, documented infection signs, a culture that identified the organism, and culture-directed antibiotics. Nothing is missing or mislabeled. It's the 'what good looks like' baseline for the acute-osteo etiology and a contrast to the chronic picture (no sequestrum/involucrum, recent onset) — including the pathway: debridement plus medical management, correctly not escalated to a CTP (osteo contraindicates) or HBOT (acute, not chronic refractory).

patient.name: Loretta Pruitt
dx: Diabetic foot ulcer, plantar right first metatarsal head, Wagner Grade 2
Limited ankle dorsiflexion (equinus); acute Charcot not excluded

radiology.finding: No osteomyelitis. (No MRI or repeat imaging obtained on the later visit when midfoot Charcot was raised as a concern.)

patient.wound_dressing: Foam dressing after sharp debridement, changed 3x/week
patient.clinical_notes: 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes (on metformin and glipizide; HbA1c 7.6%, documented and managed) and active tobacco use (~1 pack/day), seen in the wound clinic for a plantar ulcer under the right first metatarsal head, present and non-healing for about six weeks with less than 50% area reduction over that span. The wound is graded Wagner Grade 2. Peri-wound callus and thickened edges; wound bed purulent with surrounding erythema. A wound swab was obtained and culture-directed antibiotic therapy was started this visit, and the wound was sharply debrided; the infection has been identified and treatment initiated but is not yet resolved. Nutrition was assessed (albumin 3.6 g/dL, prealbumin within normal limits, dietitian consult on file). Footwear: the patient attends in regular slip-on sneakers; no total contact cast, removable boot, custom insert, or other offloading device has been prescribed or applied, and offloading is not addressed in the plan. No vascular or perfusion assessment is on file — no ABI, toe pressure (TBI), or pedal pulse exam documented. On the most recent visit the ankle showed limited passive dorsiflexion (<10 degrees, equinus) with new midfoot warmth and swelling; acute Charcot was raised as a concern, but no imaging (radiograph or MRI) was obtained to evaluate or rule it out. Plan: advance to a cellular/tissue product (skin substitute) application to close the non-healing ulcer; continue dressings and culture-directed antibiotics; recheck in two weeks.

diabetes_documented.evidence: Type 2 diabetes documented and managed (metformin + glipizide).

vascular_assessment.evidence: GAP: no perfusion assessment on file — no ABI, TBI/toe pressure, or pedal pulse exam documented. In a diabetic smoker this is the load-bearing omission (and ABI alone would be unreliable; TBI/toe pressure is needed). Perfusion is never established before advancing care.

offloading_documented.evidence: GAP: no offloading device documented — no TCC, removable boot, custom insert, or other pressure relief. Patient remains in regular sneakers; offloading is not in the plan. For a plantar DFU this is the single most important intervention.

offloading_compliance.evidence: No offloading was prescribed, so there is nothing to be compliant with — compliance can't be assessed until an offloading device is ordered.

failed_4wk_swc.evidence: GAP (the subtle one): the chart shows ~6 weeks of non-healing with <50% reduction, which looks like a documented standard-care failure — but standard wound care for a plantar DFU REQUIRES offloading, and no offloading was ever delivered. You cannot certify a failed 4-week standard-care trial when the foundational element of that care was never provided. The clock ran; the care didn't.

charcot_ruled_out.evidence: GAP: limited ankle dorsiflexion (equinus) with new midfoot warmth and swelling raised acute Charcot as a concern, but no imaging was obtained to evaluate or rule it out.

nutritional_assessment.evidence: Albumin 3.6, prealbumin WNL, dietitian consult documented.

infection_addressed.evidence: GAP (the sneaky one): infection was identified and treatment initiated this visit — wound swab, culture-directed antibiotics, sharp debridement — but the bed remains purulent with surrounding erythema and the infection is not yet resolved. L36690 requires the wound be clean and free of infection, treated and resolved, before a CTP is applied; antibiotics started does not equal infection cleared, and a skin substitute laid on an actively infected bed is not supportable.

cases.teaching_moment: Loretta's chart reads like a worked-up DFU on a quick pass — diabetes documented and controlled, a Wagner grade, a nutrition assessment with labs, infection swabbed and started on antibiotics, and now a skin substitute being advanced to close the wound. Then it falls through five independent floors, and the CTP claim dies on every one of them. First, perfusion is never established: no ABI, toe pressure, or even a pulse exam — and in a diabetic smoker that is the omission that matters most, since you cannot advance a foot wound without knowing it can heal. Second, there is no offloading — no cast, boot, or insert — for a plantar ulcer, where pressure relief is the single most important intervention. Third, and most easily missed: six weeks of non-healing looks like a documented standard-care failure, but standard care for a plantar DFU requires offloading, and offloading was never delivered — you cannot certify a failed four-week trial of care that was never actually given. Fourth, acute Charcot was suspected on the equinus and midfoot findings and never imaged or ruled out — and active Charcot is a named CTP contraindication. Fifth, the sneaky one: infection was treated but not resolved. The swab, antibiotics, and debridement make it look handled on a skim, but the bed is still purulent and antibiotics were only just started — and a CTP requires a clean wound free of infection. Antibiotics started does not equal infection cleared. Any one of these denies the CTP; together they are the lesson: a CTP claim on a DFU is a stack — diagnosis, perfusion, offloading, a valid care trial, complicating-condition workup, and a clean uninfected bed — and an auditor reads every layer, not just the ones that happen to be filled in.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The chart documents enough (diabetes, Wagner grade, glucose, nutrition) and shows visible infection treatment to read as a worked-up DFU advancing to a skin substitute — and it passes on a surface skim. Five independent holes each deny the CTP: perfusion never established (no ABI/TBI/pulse), no offloading for a plantar ulcer, no valid four-week standard-care trial (offloading was never delivered, so the documented non-healing is not a qualifying failure), acute Charcot suspected but not ruled out (a named contraindication), and infection treated but not resolved (antibiotics just started, bed still purulent — a CTP needs a clean, uninfected wound). The reason this patient’s wound remains a non-healing for six weeks with less than 50% area reduction is due to the fact that the wound has been mismanaged.  Read for what is present and you pass it; audit each required pillar and you find five floors missing.

patient.name: Inez Caldwell
dx: Chronic non-healing ulcer, right medial malleolus (atypical, autoimmune etiology)
Systemic lupus erythematosus with cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis

radiology.finding: No osteomyelitis; soft-tissue thickening at the medial malleolus only

patient.wound_dressing: Non-adherent contact layer + foam, changed 3x/week
patient.clinical_notes: 38-year-old woman with a chronic non-healing ulcer over the right medial malleolus, present about six months and originally attributed to a minor skin injury. The wound is a round, punched-out ulcer with a raised, slightly violaceous border and a red granular base with minimal discharge; mildly painful, with surrounding edema. It did not fit a venous, arterial, diabetic, or pressure pattern, and it failed to improve over several weeks of standard wound care plus a prior course of oral antibiotics, prompting a workup for an atypical cause. Vascular assessment was adequate: palpable pedal pulses bilaterally and ABI 1.0, with no arterial component (and no diabetes — HbA1c 5.3%). Autoimmune serologies were sent given the atypical, refractory presentation: ANA positive, anti-dsDNA positive, with low C3/C4 and an elevated ESR; she met SLICC criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus (with biopsy-proven membranous lupus nephritis). Because the ulcer was atypical and non-healing, a skin biopsy of the wound edge was obtained; it showed leukocytoclastic vasculitis with no evidence of malignancy, ruling out a Marjolin's-type process. When first managed for the atypical wound, the ulcer bed carried adherent fibrinous slough and devitalized tissue, which was sharply debrided to a clean base before dressing. Treatment was directed at the underlying disease — systemic corticosteroids and hydroxychloroquine — alongside local wound care, after which the wound began to granulate and contract. Plan: continue systemic immunosuppression with rheumatology as the primary treatment of the underlying disease, with local wound care including sharp debridement of devitalized tissue as needed; a cellular/tissue product is not appropriate given the active vasculitis; serial measurement.

chronicity_documented.evidence: Ulcer present ~six months, non-healing and not progressing through normal stages.

underlying_cause_workup.evidence: Big-four patterns excluded and an autoimmune cause investigated — ANA+, anti-dsDNA+, low complement → SLE per SLICC.

biopsy_if_atypical.evidence: Atypical non-healing ulcer biopsied at the edge: leukocytoclastic vasculitis, no malignancy (rules out Marjolin's).

vascular_assessment.evidence: Palpable pedal pulses bilaterally and ABI 1.0; no arterial component.

failed_4wk_swc.evidence: Failed to improve over several weeks of standard wound care plus prior oral antibiotics before the cause was found.

therapy_pathway_appropriate.evidence: The pathway is correct: the covered local procedure is debridement of devitalized tissue, paired with treatment of the identified underlying cause — systemic immunosuppression managed by rheumatology, which is what actually heals a vasculitic ulcer. A cellular/tissue product is correctly withheld: active vasculitis is a named L36690 contraindication, and the wound responds to treating the disease, not to topicals.

cases.teaching_moment: Inez is the clean baseline for the non-pressure chronic ulcer — the catch-all slot for a chronic wound whose cause isn't venous, arterial, diabetic, or pressure, done the right way. The chart earns the determination on every front: chronicity is documented (about six months, not progressing), the big-four patterns were excluded and an actual cause was investigated rather than assumed (autoimmune serologies → SLE, with low complement and a positive ANA and anti-dsDNA), perfusion was confirmed (palpable pulses, ABI 1.0), and a real standard-care failure was on record before escalation. The move that makes it defensible — and that's easy to skip — is the skin biopsy: an atypical, non-healing ulcer gets biopsied to confirm the process (leukocytoclastic vasculitis) and rule out malignancy. And the treatment lesson rides along: this wound heals when the systemic disease is treated (immunosuppression), not from topicals alone. The covered local procedure is debridement of the devitalized tissue the ulcer carried before it granulated — and a cellular/tissue product is the wrong move here: active vasculitis is a named contraindication, and a skin substitute laid over a vasculitic bed would neither qualify nor heal. When a chronic leg ulcer doesn't fit the usual buckets, this is what a properly classified and worked-up claim looks like — cause treated, devitalized tissue debrided, and the contraindicated escalation correctly left alone.
cases.difficulty_explanation: A clean, fully worked-up atypical chronic ulcer with every criterion met: documented chronicity, the big-four excluded and the true cause investigated (autoimmune → SLE), an atypical-wound biopsy that confirms the process and rules out malignancy, adequate perfusion, and a documented standard-care failure. It's the 'what good looks like' baseline for the non-pressure chronic ulcer slot — the catch-all chronic wound done right, and distinct from both a named big-four etiology and a no-call-possible documentation gap. It also carries the pathway as an audited element: debridement of devitalized tissue plus systemic disease management is the correct covered route, and a CTP is correctly withheld (active vasculitis is a named contraindication).

patient.name: Wade Pruitt
dx: Open traumatic wound with soft-tissue avulsion, lateral right lower leg
Status post all-terrain vehicle (ATV) rollover, approximately 6 weeks prior; healing by secondary intention

radiology.finding: No fracture, no cortical involvement, no retained foreign body; soft-tissue defect over the lateral lower leg

patient.wound_dressing: Negative-pressure wound therapy (NPWT) at -125 mmHg, foam changed three times weekly; interval sharp debridement of devitalized tissue
patient.clinical_notes: 47-year-old male referred to the outpatient wound care clinic for an open traumatic wound of the lateral right lower leg following an ATV rollover on 04/30/2026. In the emergency department the wound was irrigated and underwent initial debridement; a soft-tissue avulsion with devitalized muscle and subcutaneous tissue was left open to heal by secondary intention, and tetanus prophylaxis plus a short antibiotic course were completed. Right tibia/fibula radiographs at presentation showed no fracture, no cortical involvement, and no retained foreign body. Exam at the first wound care visit (05/12/2026): a 6.5 x 4.0 cm open wound over the lateral right lower leg with a ruddy granulating base, scattered residual slough, moderate serosanguinous exudate, and no exposed bone, tendon, or hardware; the wound edges are open and not approximated. The wound is healing by secondary intention and has remained open and refractory to dressing care alone. Negative-pressure wound therapy (NPWT) at -125 mmHg was initiated to accelerate granulation, with foam changes three times weekly and interval sharp debridement of devitalized tissue. Across serial visits the wound is slowly contracting but remains open and granulating. No diabetes; perfusion intact with palpable pedal pulses. Plan: continue NPWT and serial debridement until the bed is ready for closure or grafting.

mechanism_documented.evidence: ATV rollover on 04/30/2026 documented as both mechanism and date.

wound_characteristics.evidence: Location (lateral right lower leg), serial measurements, granulating base with residual slough, and serosanguinous exudate all documented.

not_primary_intention.evidence: Wound left open to heal by secondary intention, edges open and not approximated — open/refractory, not a primary-intention closure (clears the L35125 exclusion).

therapy_matches_traumatic.evidence: NPWT at -125 mmHg for accelerated granulation plus interval sharp debridement of devitalized tissue — covered therapy pair for an open traumatic wound (NPWT L32125 / debridement L37228).

cases.teaching_moment: Wade is what a clean, fully-supported traumatic-wound claim looks like — the calibration baseline for the slot. The mechanism and date are on record, the wound bed is well characterized, and the therapy pair is covered: NPWT to accelerate granulation plus serial debridement of devitalized tissue. The element that's easy to take for granted is the one that actually keeps it inside coverage — the chart explicitly establishes the wound was left open to heal by secondary intention and the edges are not approximated. A clean, incised traumatic laceration closed primarily heals by primary intention and is excluded from wound-care coverage (L35125); saying plainly that this one is open and refractory is what makes the claim defensible. The presentation radiographs ruling out fracture and cortical involvement also keep it cleanly a soft-tissue traumatic wound rather than an exposed-bone problem. Nothing to catch here — that's the point.
cases.difficulty_explanation: A clean, fully documented open traumatic wound with every criterion met: mechanism and date, a characterized wound bed, an explicit open/secondary-intention status that clears the primary-intention exclusion, and a covered NPWT-plus-debridement therapy pair. Nothing hidden — it's the 'what good looks like' anchor the family's trap cases are measured against.

patient.name: Della Rucker
dx: Dehisced abdominal surgical wound, lower midline incision (Grade 2a — subcutaneous separation with infection)
Status post open ventral hernia repair with mesh, 05/19/2026
medications: Cephalexin 500 mg four times daily (postoperative SSI course)

radiology.finding: Superficial/subcutaneous wound separation of the lower midline incision; fascia intact and continuous; no rectus sheath defect, no organ involvement, no drainable fluid collection or abscess

patient.wound_dressing: Dry gauze dressing changed daily; autologous platelet-rich plasma (PRP) gel application planned this visit
patient.clinical_notes: 58-year-old female referred to the outpatient wound care clinic for a dehisced abdominal surgical wound. She underwent open ventral hernia repair with mesh on 05/19/2026. On postoperative day 6 she developed a surgical site infection, and the lower midline incision subsequently separated. On referral, approximately 8 cm of the infraumbilical midline incision has opened to the subcutaneous layer with the fascia intact and visibly secure, consistent with a Grade 2a dehiscence (subcutaneous separation with signs of infection). Comorbidities include type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity (BMI 34), and admission labs showed a low serum albumin of 2.7 g/dL. The clinic note states the incision dehisced and is being followed, but it does not include a measured wound bed, a description of the tissue type or exudate, or serial wound measurements, and no contributing cause for the breakdown is identified or addressed in the plan of care. Plan as written: dry gauze dressing and application of autologous platelet-rich plasma (PRP) gel at this visit to promote granulation; recheck in one week.

original_surgery_documented.evidence: Open ventral hernia repair with mesh on 05/19/2026 documented (type + date).

dehiscence_documented.evidence: Subcutaneous separation of the lower midline incision documented and graded (Grade 2a, fascia intact).

wound_characteristics.evidence: The note records that the incision dehisced but provides no measured wound bed, no tissue-type or exudate description, and no serial measurements as well no follow-up on the identified infection.

cause_of_failure.evidence: Flagrant dehiscence risk factors are in the same chart — T2DM, obesity (BMI 34), hypoalbuminemia (albumin 2.7), postoperative SSI — but none is identified as a contributing cause or addressed in the plan.

therapy_matches_dehiscence.evidence: Autologous PRP gel was ordered. Autologous PRP on a dehisced/acute-surgical wound is nationally non-covered (NCD 270.3). NPWT (L32125 surgical complication) or debridement (L37228) would have been covered.

cases.teaching_moment: Della's dehisced wound is genuinely a coverable wound-care problem — a real postoperative dehiscence, fascia intact, sitting in the outpatient clinic where it belongs, and the etiology is gettable from the first two lines (documented original surgery, documented graded separation). The claim still falls apart in three independent places. First, the wound is never characterized: no measured bed, no tissue type, no exudate, no serial measurements and no follow-up on identified infection — coverage and medical necessity for ongoing wound care can't be built from 'the incision dehisced and is being followed.' Second, the cause of the breakdown is staring off the same page and is never named or managed — uncontrolled diabetes, obesity, an albumin of 2.7, and a postoperative infection are textbook dehiscence drivers, and a plan that doesn't identify and address them won't support continued treatment or heal the wound. Third, and most concrete: the ordered therapy is autologous platelet-rich plasma, which is nationally non-covered for this kind of wound (NCD 270.3). The fix isn't a different diagnosis — it's a measured wound bed, a named-and-addressed cause, and a covered therapy (NPWT or debridement) in place of the PRP.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The etiology is right and easy to get; the denial is a stack, not a single miss. Three independent coverage holes — an uncharacterized wound bed, an unaddressed (and clearly documented) cause of failure, and a nationally non-covered therapy (PRP, NCD 270.3) — each enough to sink the claim on its own. The L4 skill isn't spotting one gap; it's auditing every required element and counting how many are missing.

patient.name: Floyd Beasley
dx: Surgical wound dehiscence with fascial separation and exposed bowel, lower midline laparotomy incision (Sandy Grade 4a)
Status post emergency Hartmann procedure for perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with generalized peritonitis, 06/01/2026
Postoperative surgical site infection with deep/organ-space involvement

radiology.finding: Midline fascial separation with loops of small bowel exposed at the wound base and communicating with the peritoneal cavity; no organized drainable abscess; postoperative changes consistent with recent Hartmann procedure

patient.wound_dressing: Saline-moistened gauze packing; exposed bowel covered with a non-adherent contact layer
patient.clinical_notes: 70-year-old male seen on the inpatient surgical service for consideration of wound care management of a dehisced abdominal incision. He underwent an emergency Hartmann procedure for perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with generalized peritonitis on 06/01/2026. On postoperative day 9 the midline incision developed worsening erythema and purulent drainage; complete suture removal revealed fascial dehiscence with loops of small bowel visible and partially exposed at the wound base, communicating with the peritoneal cavity. The wound bed contains necrotic and fibrinous tissue with copious purulent exudate; the patient is febrile with leukocytosis and remains on intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics. CT confirms fascial separation with exposed bowel and no organized drainable collection. The wound is currently packed with saline-moistened gauze and the exposed bowel is covered with a non-adherent contact layer. Comorbidities include type 2 diabetes mellitus and COPD. Plan as written by the covering team: consult outpatient wound care to initiate negative-pressure wound therapy and assume ongoing dressing management.

cases.teaching_moment: Floyd's chart pulls hard toward a wound-care call — there's a dehisced surgical incision, a characterizable bed, and an order to start NPWT, which looks like an ordinary dehiscence case. Stop at what's actually exposed. This is fascial dehiscence with loops of bowel exposed at the wound base and communicating with the peritoneal cavity (Sandy Grade 4a), in a febrile, septic, postoperative patient still on intravenous antibiotics. That is an acute inpatient surgical problem, not an outpatient wound-care claim: placing NPWT foam directly on exposed bowel risks perforation and enterocutaneous fistula, and the wound needs operative management and inpatient-level care under the surgical service. Negative-pressure therapy may well be used here — but as inpatient, surgeon-directed therapy with bowel protection, not as an outpatient wound-care encounter that gets billed. The correct call is Not a WC Pathway: this stays with the inpatient surgical team. Running it as an outpatient dehiscence claim is both a wrong-pathway denial and a patient-safety error — the most gradeable-looking feature, a dehisced surgical wound, is exactly the bait.
cases.difficulty_explanation: Every surface cue says dehisced surgical wound: a separated incision, a packable bed, an order to start NPWT. The whole case is the exposure underneath — fascial dehiscence with bowel visible and communicating with the peritoneal cavity in a septic postoperative patient — which reroutes the wound out of the outpatient pathway to inpatient surgical management. You don't grade this wound; you recognize it isn't an outpatient claim. The most gradeable-looking finding is the bait.

patient.name: Orval Sizemore
dx: Non-healing surgical wound, mid-incision dehiscence, right knee
Status post right total knee arthroplasty, 04/14/2026
Underlying vascular insufficiency (note: 'vasculopathic venostasis'), not yet worked up

radiology.finding: Total knee arthroplasty components well-seated; no periprosthetic lucency, loosening, or hardware complication; soft-tissue defect over the mid-incision

patient.wound_dressing: Dry dressing with intermittent compression wrap; cellular/tissue skin-substitute graft planned this week
patient.clinical_notes: 76-year-old male followed within the orthopedic service for right total knee arthroplasty performed 04/14/2026. At staple removal the mid-portion of the surgical incision showed dehiscence and was referred to the wound center for a non-healing surgical wound at the right knee. History notable for COPD, hyperlipidemia, essential hypertension, and a 40-pack-year smoking history (current smoker). Over the following six weeks of conservative care (dressings, intermittent compression, oral antibiotics) the wound failed to heal. Exam at the wound check: a 4 cm x 3 cm full-thickness wound at the mid-incision with undermining toward the underlying patellar tissue; base with mixed granulation and early necrosis, moderate serous exudate. The surrounding limb is described in the note as showing 'vasculopathic venostasis.' No ankle-brachial index, toe pressures, pedal-pulse exam, or venous duplex study is recorded, and the underlying vascular status is not otherwise worked up or addressed in the plan. Originally the wound was managed by the operating orthopedic surgeon as part of post-arthroplasty follow-up. Plan as written: take to the OR for irrigation and apply a cellular/tissue skin-substitute graft to the wound this week.

original_surgery_documented.evidence: Right total knee arthroplasty on 04/14/2026 documented (type + date).

wound_characteristics.evidence: Location, serial measurements, full-thickness depth, mobile flap with undermining, tissue type, and exudate all documented.

refractory_healing.evidence: Dehiscence that failed six weeks of conservative care and is not progressing across serial measurements — refractory/complicated, the coverage trigger.

separately_coverable_not_global.evidence: No transfer agreement is stated in the patient’s record.

cause_of_failure.evidence: Underlying 'vasculopathic venostasis' is named and the patient is a high arterial-risk 40-pack-year smoker with COPD, but there is no ABI/toe pressure/pulse exam/venous study and nothing in the plan addresses the vascular driver before escalating to a graft.

cases.teaching_moment: Orval's wound clears the bar that matters most for a surgical-wound claim — it's genuinely refractory: a documented dehiscence that failed six weeks of conservative care and isn't progressing, well characterized with measurements, undermining, and tissue description. That makes Surgical Wound the right call, and escalating to advanced therapy looks reasonable. The cause of failure is named but never worked up: the note labels the limb 'vasculopathic venostasis,' and the patient is a 76-year-old, 40-pack-year current smoker with COPD — a textbook arterial-risk profile — yet there is no ABI, no toe pressure, no pulse exam, and no venous study anywhere, and nothing in the plan addresses the vascular driver before grafting. You can't establish the cause of delayed healing (or safely apply a skin substitute) without it; if perfusion is poor, the graft fails and you may be grafting an ischemic limb. The fix isn't a different diagnosis: it's a documented vascular workup that identifies and addresses the underlying cause. A documented hand-off from the operating surgeon's global package to wound care should be included in the patient’s record, with the ongoing treatment charted as management of the underlying vascular condition and a distinct course beyond routine post-arthroplasty recovery — the pieces that move it out of the bundled 90-day global period (Medicare Global Surgery guidance, MLN907166). Depending on who assumes care, that hand-off is carried by the transfer-of-care modifiers (54 surgical-care-only / 55 post-operative-management-only, under a written transfer agreement) and, since December 2024, the add-on code G0559 for post-operative care by a practitioner other than the operating surgeon.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The etiology is right and the coverage trigger (refractory, failed conservative care) is genuinely met, so the case reads like reasonable escalation. The underlying cause of failure is named but never worked up or addressed (no perfusion or venous assessment in a high arterial-risk patient).

patient.name: Glenda Hatfield
dx: Non-healing dehisced surgical wound, lower midline abdomen
Status post exploratory laparotomy with small bowel resection for adhesive small bowel obstruction, 02/16/2026
Superficial wound dehiscence, healing by secondary intention

radiology.finding: Superficial subcutaneous separation of the lower midline incision; fascia intact and continuous; no abscess or fluid collection

patient.wound_dressing: Moist wound dressing changed daily; cellular/tissue skin-substitute graft planned this visit
patient.clinical_notes: 66-year-old female referred to the outpatient wound care clinic for a non-healing dehisced surgical wound of the lower midline abdomen. She underwent exploratory laparotomy with small bowel resection for adhesive small bowel obstruction on 02/16/2026; the lower midline incision developed a superficial dehiscence postoperatively and has been managed with dressing care since. Now approximately 16 weeks out and well past the surgical global period, she was referred to the wound care clinic for ongoing management. Exam: a 4.7 x 2.4 cm open wound at the lower midline with a clean granulating base, scant serous exudate, and no necrosis; fascia intact on prior CT with no collection. Across serial measurements over the past several weeks the wound has been slowly contracting on standard dressing care. Contributing factors — the postoperative dehiscence and well-controlled type 2 diabetes (A1c 6.9%) — are identified and being optimized. There is no documentation of a failed trial of standard wound care; the wound has, if anything, been improving. Plan as written: apply a cellular/tissue skin-substitute graft at this visit to speed closure.

original_surgery_documented.evidence: Exploratory laparotomy with small bowel resection on 02/16/2026 documented (type + date).

wound_characteristics.evidence: Lower-midline location, serial measurements, clean granulating base, scant serous exudate documented.

refractory_healing.evidence: No documented failure of standard wound care — serial measurements show the wound slowly improving on ordinary dressing care. The coverage trigger for advancing to a skin substitute (a documented adequate trial of standard care that failed) is not met.

separately_coverable_not_global.evidence: Approximately 16 weeks out, well past the 90-day surgical global period, and referred to the outpatient wound care clinic — separately coverable, not routine global-period postop.

cause_of_failure.evidence: Contributing factors (postoperative dehiscence, well-controlled diabetes) are identified and being optimized in the plan of care.

cases.teaching_moment: Glenda's chart looks like a complete, reasonable surgical-wound claim ready to escalate: the original surgery is documented with a date, the wound is well characterized and measured serially, the care is properly past the global period and referred to the wound care clinic, and contributing factors are identified and being managed.
