Pick the etiology and it's plainly a surgical wound. The quiet problem is the one thing that actually authorizes the next step: there is no documented failure of standard wound care. In fact the serial measurements show the wound slowly improving on ordinary dressing care — and the plan still indicates the use of a cellular/tissue skin substitute. Advanced therapies like a CTP are covered only after an adequate trial of standard wound care has been tried and documented to fail; a wound that is progressing on conservative care has not met that trigger, so the graft is both premature clinically and a denial on review. The fix isn't a new diagnosis or more workup — it's continuing and documenting the standard-care course, and only escalating (with the failure documented) if the wound actually stalls.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The chart reads thorough and the etiology is obvious: documented surgery, a measured and characterized wound, proper referral past the global period, identified contributing factors. The single silent gap is the coverage trigger for the very therapy being ordered — there's no documented failure of standard wound care, and the wound is actually improving. In addition, getting a dehisced surgical wound to qualify even if it were failing would require extensive documentation to meet the medically necessary requirements that CMS is looking for.

patient.name: Buford Tackett
dx: Chronic non-healing wound with exposed orthopedic hardware, distal left tibia / medial ankle
Remote left pilon fracture, status post open reduction and internal fixation
Severe peripheral arterial disease, left lower extremity (ABI 0.55, single-vessel runoff)

radiology.finding: Medial and lateral fixation hardware intact and well-seated; no periprosthetic lucency or radiographic osteomyelitis
Diffuse superficial femoral artery disease, occluded popliteal artery, single-vessel posterior tibial runoff to the foot

patient.wound_dressing: Daily dressing changes; cellular/tissue skin-substitute graft planned this visit
patient.clinical_notes: 61-year-old male referred to the outpatient wound care clinic for a chronic non-healing wound with exposed hardware over the distal left tibia and medial ankle. He has a remote history of a left pilon fracture treated with open reduction and internal fixation; a minor work injury several months ago reopened the soft tissue, and the wound has been present roughly three months with progressively exposed orthopedic hardware. He has severe peripheral arterial disease — a 30-pack-year smoking history, one-block calf claudication, absent pedal pulses, and an ankle-brachial index of 0.55 on the left with single-vessel runoff to the foot on prior angiography. Exam: a 6 x 2 cm wound over the distal tibia with metal hardware visible and probe-able at the base, scant serous exudate, and granulation at the margins; no surrounding cellulitis. The wound was evaluated for deep infection and hardware-associated osteomyelitis; there are no clinical signs of infection and imaging shows intact hardware without osteomyelitis. Orthopedics was consulted and documented options for hardware removal versus retention; vascular surgery documented the severe PAD and limited revascularization options. Plan as written: apply a cellular/tissue skin-substitute graft over the wound this visit to achieve coverage and closure.

hardware_exposure_documented.evidence: Exposed orthopedic hardware over the distal tibia documented, visible and probe-able at the wound base, from a remote pilon-fracture open reduction and internal fixation.

wound_characteristics.evidence: Distal-tibia location, serial measurements (6 x 2 cm), granulating margins, scant serous exudate documented.

infection_evaluation.evidence: Deep infection and hardware-associated osteomyelitis evaluated and excluded — no clinical signs of infection, no osteomyelitis on imaging.

surgical_consult.evidence: Orthopedics consulted and documented hardware removal vs. retention; vascular surgery documented the PAD and revascularization options.

perfusion_adequate.evidence: ABI 0.55 on the left, with absent pedal pulses and single-vessel runoff — below L36690's perfusion floor of 0.60 for a CTP. Inadequate circulation to support a graft, so the claim is not supportable (and clinically the graft would not take) until perfusion is addressed. The exposed hardware is not the bar — some skin substitutes are labeled for exposed structures — the perfusion is.

cases.teaching_moment: Buford's wound is defined by what is at its base — exposed orthopedic hardware from an old pilon-fracture fixation — so the indication is a wound with exposed hardware, and the chart is otherwise strong: hardware documented and probe-able, wound measured and characterized, deep infection and osteomyelitis evaluated and excluded, orthopedics and vascular surgery both consulted. The scary ABI tempts you to call this arterial, but the wound's etiology is the hardware (a traumatic ORIF site with granulating margins, not a punched-out distal arterial ulcer); the arterial disease is the comorbidity — and that comorbidity is what kills the claim. Medicare requires adequate circulation for a CTP, an ABI of no less than 0.60. Buford's is 0.55, with absent pedal pulses and single-vessel runoff — below the floor. There is not enough perfusion to support a graft, so a CTP is neither covered nor clinically able to take until the perfusion is addressed (revascularization, vascular-directed management). Furthermore, there are no FDA approved CTPs that can go over exposed hardware.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The etiology is gettable but baited: exposed hardware is the defining feature, while the severe arterial disease tempts a wrong ARTERIAL pick. The chart looks thorough — hardware documented, wound characterized, infection excluded, consults placed — so the order reads reasonable. The miss is the perfusion: ABI 0.55 is below 0.60 floor, so a CTP is not supportable on this limb.

patient.name: Dewey Stanton
dx: Acute severe flame burns, approximately 28% total body surface area (mixed deep partial and full thickness), bilateral upper extremities, both hands, and anterior chest
Status post gasoline ignition (flame burn), 2 days prior

radiology.finding: No acute infiltrate or pulmonary edema; clinical concern for inhalation injury noted (hoarse voice, singed nasal hair)

patient.wound_dressing: Silver sulfadiazine and sterile burn dressings; outpatient wound care follow-up with consideration of skin-substitute application proposed
patient.clinical_notes: 58-year-old male transferred from a community emergency department two days after sustaining flame burns when gasoline ignited while he was working on equipment. Burns involve the bilateral upper extremities, both hands, and the anterior chest, estimated at approximately 28% total body surface area, with mixed deep partial-thickness and full-thickness areas (leathery, insensate eschar over portions of the forearms and dorsal hands). He required initial fluid resuscitation and developed a transient acute kidney injury. Pain is significant and managed with intravenous analgesia; tetanus prophylaxis was given. There is no documented airway compromise, but a hoarse voice and singed nasal hair were noted at the referring facility, raising concern for inhalation injury. The full-thickness areas will require surgical excision and autografting, and the hand involvement raises functional and contracture concerns. Plan as written by the covering team: arrange outpatient wound care follow-up for ongoing burn dressing changes and consider application of a cellular/tissue skin substitute to the burn wounds to promote closure.

cases.teaching_moment: This chart is an acute burn, and the dropdown has a Burn option — which is exactly the bait. An acute, significant burn is not an outpatient wound-care pathway. This is roughly 28% total body surface area with full-thickness, insensate eschar over the forearms and hands, recent fluid resuscitation and a transient acute kidney injury, and findings that raise an inhalation concern (hoarse voice, singed nasal hair). Burns of this depth and extent — and burns involving the hands and other functional areas — are managed at a regional burn center: surgical excision and autografting, specialized critical and rehabilitative care, and contracture prevention. A cellular/tissue skin substitute is neither the covered nor the appropriate treatment for an acute full-thickness burn, which needs autograft, and 'outpatient burn dressings plus a CTP' both undertreats the patient and is a wrong-pathway claim. The correct call is Not a WC Pathway: transfer or refer to a burn center. Picking Burn and grading or treating it as a wound-care claim is the error; recognizing it belongs elsewhere is the skill.
cases.difficulty_explanation: A burn is right there in the chart and Burn is right there in the dropdown, so the tempting move is to pick it and grade. The whole case is recognizing that an acute significant burn — large TBSA, full-thickness eschar, hand involvement, an inhalation concern — is burn-center care, not an outpatient wound-care claim, and that a skin substitute is neither the covered nor the appropriate therapy. You don't grade this wound; you reroute it.

patient.name: Maxine Caldwell
dx: Chronic venous insufficiency, bilateral lower extremities
Venous stasis ulcer, left medial lower leg

radiology.study: Venous duplex ultrasound, left lower extremity
radiology.finding: Great saphenous vein reflux 2.0 s; deep venous system patent, no DVT
ABI 1.0; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable — no significant arterial component

patient.wound_dressing: Full multilayer compression wrap (Profore), changed weekly; foam primary dressing
patient.clinical_notes: 68-year-old non-smoking female referred to the outpatient wound care clinic for a non-healing venous stasis ulcer of the left medial lower leg, first documented 02/20/2026 (now approximately 16 weeks). History of chronic venous insufficiency. Exam: an ulcer over the medial gaiter region with an irregular shallow border, ruddy granular base, scant serous exudate, and no necrosis; surrounding hemosiderin staining and lipodermatosclerosis; 2+ pitting edema; visible varicosities. Venous duplex ultrasound on 02/24/2026 confirmed great saphenous vein reflux (2.0 s); deep system patent, no DVT. Arterial perfusion is documented and adequate: ankle-brachial index 1.0 with palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, which rules out a significant arterial component and clears the limb for compression. CEAP class C6; VCSS 13. Full multilayer compression was initiated 02/27/2026 with weekly changes plus leg elevation, and edema is managed. Over more than four weeks of documented standard care the wound shows less than 50% area reduction; the wound is clean, granular, and greater than 1 cm squared. Plan: continue full compression and advance to a cellular/tissue skin substitute at this visit, with all coverage criteria documented.

venous_reflux_studies.evidence: Venous duplex 02/24/2026 confirms great saphenous reflux — venous etiology established.

abi_supports_venous.evidence: ABI 1.0 with palpable pedal pulses documented — rules out a significant arterial component and confirms the etiology is venous.

compression_ordered.evidence: Full multilayer compression initiated 02/27/2026, weekly changes.

compression_appropriate_for_abi.evidence: ABI 1.0 documented before compression — perfusion is adequate, so full compression is appropriate and safe.

edema_managed.evidence: 2+ pitting edema managed with compression plus leg elevation.

ceap_vcss.evidence: CEAP class C6 and VCSS 13 documented.

wound_characteristics_venous.evidence: Medial gaiter location, hemosiderin staining, irregular shallow border — textbook venous.

failed_4wk_swc.evidence: More than four weeks of documented standard care with <50% area reduction across serial measurements.

dx_over_3mo.evidence: Venous ulcer documented since 02/20/2026 (~16 weeks, > 3 months).

cases.teaching_moment: Maxine is what a clean, fully-supported venous claim looks like — the calibration baseline for the slot. Every criterion is met and documented: a duplex confirming reflux, CEAP C6 and VCSS 13, more than three months' duration, a real four-week standard-care failure on record, and a clean qualifying wound greater than 1 cm squared. The element that's easy to take for granted — and the one that quietly sinks venous claims when it's missing — is the perfusion: an ABI of 1.0 with palpable pulses is documented before compression, which both confirms the etiology is venous (not arterial or mixed) and certifies that full compression is safe. Edema is managed with compression and elevation, the wound is characterized at the classic medial gaiter location with hemosiderin staining, and the four-week failure is documented before escalating to a skin substitute. When every gate is met and written down, this is the claim that gets paid — and the wound that actually heals.
cases.difficulty_explanation: A clean, fully worked-up venous ulcer with every criterion met and documented: confirmed reflux, documented adequate perfusion (ABI 1.0) that clears compression, full compression with edema management, CEAP/VCSS, a documented standard-care failure, and a qualifying wound over three months old. Nothing to catch — it's the 'what good looks like' venous anchor the trap cases are measured against.

patient.name: Hershel Combs

patient.clinical_notes: 71-year-old male referred to the outpatient wound care clinic for a painful non-healing ulcer of the right lateral foot at the fifth metatarsal head and toe. Exam: a small, well-demarcated ulcer with a punched-out border and a pale, dry base; the wound and surrounding foot are painful, worse with elevation and at night, with diminished hair growth and dependent rubor. Arterial perfusion is documented and consistent with lower-extremity arterial disease: ankle-brachial index 0.62 on the right with monophasic Doppler signals and diminished pedal pulses. Given the arterial status, compression is appropriately withheld. Vascular surgery referral was placed for revascularization evaluation. The history of the current wound and prior treatments (local wound care, offloading footwear) is documented. The patient was counseled on smoking cessation and started on a cessation plan. wound_characteristics_arterial.evidence: Distal foot/toe location, punched-out well-demarcated border, pale dry base, painful — textbook arterial.

compression_avoided.evidence: Compression appropriately withheld given the arterial status (contraindicated at low ABI).

vascular_referral.evidence: Vascular surgery referral placed for revascularization evaluation.

history_prior_treatment.evidence: History of the current wound and prior treatments (local wound care, offloading) documented.

infection_addressed.evidence: Wound assessed for infection; no clinical signs of infection at this time.

cases.teaching_moment: Hershel is what a clean, fully-documented arterial ulcer looks like — the calibration baseline for the slot. The etiology is established the right way: a documented ABI of 0.62 with monophasic signals and diminished pulses, on a painful, punched-out distal ulcer with dependent rubor. The arterial-specific move that defines good care here is what's withheld: compression is appropriately held off given the arterial status, because compressing an ischemic limb causes harm. A vascular surgery referral is placed for revascularization evaluation — the treatment that actually addresses an arterial ulcer — and the wound history, prior treatments, smoking cessation, and infection assessment are all documented. When the perfusion is documented, compression is correctly avoided, and the referral is made and written down, this is what a supported arterial claim looks like.
cases.difficulty_explanation: A clean, fully worked-up arterial ulcer with every criterion met and documented: perfusion established by ABI (LEAD), classic arterial wound characteristics, compression correctly withheld, vascular referral placed, history and prior treatment recorded, tobacco addressed, infection assessed. Nothing to catch — it's the 'what good looks like' arterial anchor, and the place to learn that with arterial the right move is often what you don't do.

patient.name: Lorene Maddox
dx: Mixed arterial and venous lower-extremity ulcer, right medial lower leg

radiology.study: Venous duplex ultrasound, right lower extremity
radiology.finding: Great saphenous vein reflux 2.1 s; no DVT
ABI 0.72; monophasic waveforms; diminished pedal pulses — moderate arterial component

patient.wound_dressing: Reduced (modified) compression wrap, changed weekly; foam primary dressing
patient.clinical_notes: 70-year-old female referred to the outpatient wound care clinic for a non-healing ulcer of the right medial lower leg with features of both venous and arterial disease. History of chronic venous insufficiency and peripheral arterial disease. Exam: an ulcer over the medial gaiter region with an irregular border and a partly pale base; surrounding hemosiderin staining and lipodermatosclerosis with mild dependent rubor; 1+ edema. Venous duplex confirmed great saphenous reflux (2.1 s) with no DVT, documenting the venous component. Arterial perfusion is documented and reduced: ankle-brachial index 0.72 on the right with monophasic signals and diminished pedal pulses — a significant arterial component that does not contraindicate compression outright but does require it to be adjusted. Accordingly, compression was modified — reduced rather than full — given the arterial component, and vascular surgery referral was placed for arterial evaluation. Over more than four weeks of documented standard care the wound shows less than 50% area reduction. Plan: continue reduced compression, complete the vascular evaluation, and ongoing wound care.

arterial_component_documented.evidence: ABI 0.72 with monophasic signals and diminished pulses documented — the arterial component is established.

venous_component_documented.evidence: Venous duplex confirms great saphenous reflux with hemosiderin staining — the venous component is established.

compression_modified_for_arterial.evidence: Given the arterial component (ABI 0.72), compression was modified — reduced rather than full — instead of standard full compression.

vascular_referral.evidence: Vascular surgery referral placed for arterial evaluation.

wound_characteristics_mixed.evidence: Medial gaiter location with venous stigmata plus an irregular, partly pale base and dependent rubor — features of both.

failed_4wk_swc.evidence: More than four weeks of documented standard care with <50% area reduction.

cases.teaching_moment: Lorene is what a clean mixed arterial/venous ulcer looks like when both halves of the problem are actually documented and acted on. The venous component is established with a duplex showing reflux and the surrounding hemosiderin and lipodermatosclerosis; the arterial component is established with a documented ABI of 0.72, monophasic signals, and diminished pulses. The move that defines good mixed-disease care — and the one that causes real harm when it's skipped — is the compression decision: with a significant arterial component, compression is not applied at full strength, but it isn't simply abandoned either; here it's correctly modified to reduced compression, and a vascular referral is placed to evaluate the arterial side. The wound shows features of both etiologies at the gaiter region, and a four-week standard-care failure is documented. When both components are documented and the compression is matched to the perfusion, this is the mixed claim that's both supported and safe.
cases.difficulty_explanation: A clean, fully worked-up mixed arterial/venous ulcer with every criterion met: both components documented (duplex reflux + ABI 0.72), compression correctly modified for the arterial component rather than applied full or withheld entirely, a vascular referral placed, mixed wound characteristics, and a documented standard-care failure. Nothing to catch — it's the mixed-disease 'what good looks like' anchor, and the place to learn that the compression decision in mixed disease is a dial, not a switch.

patient.name: Garnet Sellers

radiology.finding: Sacral soft-tissue defect without rim-enhancing collection; no marrow signal changes to suggest osteomyelitis

He is on a low-air-loss support surface, with a documented turning and repositioning schedule every two hours. A nutritional assessment was completed with a dietitian consult; albumin was 2.9 g/dL and current pre-albumin is within normal limits, also protein supplementation was started for protein-calorie malnutrition. Plan: continue the support surface, repositioning, moisture and incontinence management, nutritional optimization, and local wound care.

stage_documented.evidence: Stage IV pressure injury staged and trended with serial NPIAP scoring.

location_bony_prominence.evidence: Located over the sacrum, a bony prominence.

pressure_etiology.evidence: Pressure and shear from immobility documented and distinguished from moisture-associated skin damage.

repositioning.evidence: Documented turning and repositioning schedule every two hours.

moisture_incontinence_managed.evidence: Documented moisture/incontinence plan: scheduled toileting/cleansing, barrier protectant, containment products.

nutritional_assessment.evidence: Dietitian consult with albumin 2.9 and protein supplementation for malnutrition.

cases.teaching_moment: Garnet is what a fully-supported pressure injury claim looks like — the calibration baseline for the slot. The wound is staged and trended (Stage IV, NPIAP), it sits over a bony prominence, and the etiology is explicitly pressure and shear from immobility, deliberately distinguished from moisture-associated skin damage. The care bundle that medical necessity rests on is all present and written down: a low-air-loss support surface, a two-hourly repositioning schedule, a nutritional assessment with a dietitian consult and protein supplementation, and — the element that quietly sinks otherwise-thorough pressure claims — a documented moisture and incontinence management plan, which matters enormously in a doubly-incontinent patient with a sacral wound. When the staging, the surface, the turning, the nutrition, and the moisture plan are all documented, this is the pressure-injury claim that's supported and the wound that has a chance to heal.
cases.difficulty_explanation: A clean, fully documented Stage IV pressure injury with every criterion met: staging with NPIAP, bony-prominence location, pressure/shear etiology distinguished from MASD, support surface, repositioning, nutritional assessment, and a documented moisture/incontinence plan. Nothing to catch — it's the pressure-injury 'what good looks like' anchor, and the place to see the moisture/incontinence element present rather than silently absent.

patient.name: Burl Whitaker
dx: Diabetic foot ulcer, plantar right first metatarsal head (Wagner Grade 2)
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy

radiology.finding: No osteomyelitis, no cortical destruction; no fragmentation or joint disorganization to suggest Charcot

patient.wound_dressing: Total contact cast, changed weekly; collagen primary dressing
patient.clinical_notes: 62-year-old male with type 2 diabetes and peripheral neuropathy, seen for a plantar diabetic foot ulcer at the right first metatarsal head. The ulcer is graded Wagner Grade 2 and has been present about seven weeks. Loss of protective sensation is confirmed on Semmes-Weinstein monofilament testing. The wound is offloaded in a total contact cast applied since 04/28/2026, and the patient is documented as compliant with the cast and follow-up. Glycemic control is documented with an HbA1c of 7.3%. Foot radiographs show no osteomyelitis and no fragmentation or joint disorganization, so Charcot is excluded. A nutritional assessment was completed (albumin 3.6 g/dL, adequate intake). The wound has no clinical signs of infection and none is being treated. Over more than four weeks of documented standard care the ulcer shows less than 50% area reduction. There is no ankle-brachial index, toe pressure, or pedal-pulse examination recorded anywhere in the chart, and perfusion is not otherwise documented. Plan: apply a cellular/tissue skin substitute at this visit to advance closure.

diabetes_documented.evidence: Type 2 diabetes with neuropathy documented; on insulin and metformin.

vascular_assessment.evidence: No ABI, toe pressure, or pedal-pulse exam is recorded and perfusion is not otherwise documented — in a diabetic (where vessels may be calcified) you cannot confirm adequate perfusion before a CTP, and arterial/neuroischemic disease isn't ruled out.

offloading_documented.evidence: Total contact cast in place since 04/28/2026.

offloading_compliance.evidence: Documented compliant with the cast and follow-up.

failed_4wk_swc.evidence: More than four weeks of documented standard care with <50% area reduction.

charcot_ruled_out.evidence: Radiographs show no fragmentation/joint disorganization — Charcot excluded.

nutritional_assessment.evidence: Nutritional assessment with albumin 3.6 and adequate intake.

infection_addressed.evidence: No clinical signs of infection; none being treated.

cases.teaching_moment: Burl's chart is a strong DFU workup and reads like it's ready to escalate: the ulcer is Wagner-graded, loss of protective sensation is confirmed, it's offloaded in a total contact cast with documented compliance, glycemic control is on record, Charcot is excluded on film, nutrition is assessed, and there's no infection — with a documented four-week standard-care failure. He clears nearly every CTP gate. The one that's silently missing is perfusion: there is no ABI, toe pressure, or pulse exam anywhere in the chart. CMS requires documented adequate perfusion before a skin substitute, and in a diabetic foot that step is doubly important — neuropathy can mask ischemic pain, and calcified vessels can make a standard ABI falsely reassuring (which is exactly why toe pressures or a TBI are used). Without it the CTP is denied on review, and clinically you may be grafting a neuroischemic foot. The diagnosis is right and the workup looks complete; the missing number is the catch.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The diagnosis is right and the chart is thorough: Wagner grade, monofilament, offloading with compliance, glycemic control, Charcot excluded, nutrition, a documented failure. The single silent gap is perfusion — no ABI, toe pressure, or pulse exam — which both clears the CTP and rules out a neuroischemic foot. Read for what's present and you pass it; audit for the one required element that isn't there and you catch it.

patient.name: Alvin Sluder
dx: Diabetic foot ulcer, lateral left foot (referring diagnosis)
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy
Peripheral arterial disease, left lower extremity

radiology.study: Arterial duplex / ABI, left lower extremity
radiology.finding: ABI 0.55; monophasic waveforms; absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses — severe lower-extremity arterial disease
No osteomyelitis; no Charcot changes

patient.wound_dressing: Dry protective dressing; cellular/tissue skin-substitute graft planned this visit
patient.clinical_notes: 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and peripheral neuropathy, referred for a non-healing foot ulcer carried in the chart as a diabetic foot ulcer. The ulcer is on the lateral aspect of the left foot near the fifth toe — not a plantar pressure point — with a punched-out, well-demarcated border and a pale, dry base. Unlike a typical painless neuropathic ulcer it is painful, worse at night and with elevation, and the foot shows dependent rubor with thin, shiny skin and absent hair growth. Pulses are absent at the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial; an ankle-brachial index was obtained and is 0.55 on the left with monophasic Doppler signals, documenting severe lower-extremity arterial disease. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and was counseled on cessation. Prior treatment has included local wound care and offloading footwear, documented in the history. The wound was assessed for infection with no current signs of infection. There is no vascular surgery referral on file. Plan as written: advance the diabetic foot ulcer to a cellular/tissue skin substitute at this visit to promote closure.

arterial_perfusion_documented.evidence: ABI 0.55 with monophasic signals and absent pulses is documented — perfusion is established and shows severe LEAD; this is the arterial etiology, not a neuropathic DFU.

wound_characteristics_arterial.evidence: Lateral non-plantar location, punched-out border, pale dry base, painful with dependent rubor — arterial morphology, atypical for a pressure-point DFU.

compression_avoided.evidence: Compression is not a factor for this distal foot ulcer.

vascular_referral.evidence: ABI 0.55 with absent pulses is severe arterial disease and a clear indication for vascular referral, but none is on file — and instead a graft is planned, which cannot take on an ischemic limb.

history_prior_treatment.evidence: History of the current wound and prior treatment (local wound care, offloading) documented.

tobacco_status.evidence: 40-pack-year tobacco use documented with cessation counseling.

infection_addressed.evidence: Assessed for infection; no current signs.

cases.teaching_moment: Alvin's ulcer is carried as a diabetic foot ulcer because he's diabetic — with the chart describing an arterial insufficiency, and the plan to graft it is the danger. The tells are all there: the ulcer sits on the lateral foot; it's punched-out and painful; the foot has dependent rubor and absent pulses; and an ABI of 0.55 with monophasic signals documents severe arterial disease. Unlike the case where the number is never obtained, here it was obtained, it's clearly bad, and the diagnosis and plan ignore it. The correct etiology is arterial, the right next step is a vascular referral for revascularization — which isn't on file — and a cellular/tissue skin substitute is exactly the wrong move: a graft cannot take on a limb without perfusion, so it's both a non-covered/miscoded claim and a clinical harm. The lesson is to read the wound the chart describes, not the label the chart assigns.
cases.difficulty_explanation: A lateral, punched-out, painful ulcer with absent pulses and a documented ABI of 0.55 indicates that the wound is caused by arterial insufficiency. The skill is overriding the label to pick the right etiology — and recognizing that grafting an ischemic limb is the kill-shot, not reasonable escalation. The contraindication sting: the worse the perfusion, the more wrong the planned CTP.

patient.name: Etta Coffey
dx: Peripheral arterial disease, left lower extremity (ABI 0.58)

radiology.study: Arterial duplex / ABI, left lower extremity
radiology.finding: ABI 0.58; monophasic waveforms; diminished distal pulses — significant lower-extremity arterial disease
No osteomyelitis; no acute osseous abnormality

patient.wound_dressing: Dry non-adherent dressing
patient.clinical_notes: 71-year-old woman seen for a chronic, painful ulcer over the left lateral malleolus, correctly worked up as an arterial (ischemic) ulcer. The wound has a punched-out, well-demarcated border with a pale, dry base; the surrounding skin is thin and shiny with absent hair, and the leg is cool with dependent rubor. Pulses are diminished; an ankle-brachial index of 0.58 with monophasic Doppler signals documents significant lower-extremity arterial disease. Given the arterial disease, compression therapy was appropriately withheld. The wound was assessed and shows no current signs of infection. She is an active smoker; no cessation counseling is documented at this visit. There is no vascular surgery referral on file despite the documented ischemia. The history does not document any prior course of conservative wound care or a trial of standard treatment before this visit. Plan: continue local dressings and reassess.

arterial_perfusion_documented.evidence: ABI 0.58 with monophasic signals and diminished pulses documents the arterial etiology.

wound_characteristics_arterial.evidence: Punched-out, pale, painful ulcer over the lateral malleolus with dependent rubor — arterial morphology.

compression_avoided.evidence: Compression therapy appropriately withheld given the arterial disease.

vascular_referral.evidence: ABI 0.58 with diminished pulses is significant ischemia and an indication for vascular referral, but none is on file — and revascularization is the actual treatment for an arterial ulcer.

history_prior_treatment.evidence: No prior course of conservative wound care or a standard-treatment trial is documented before this visit.

tobacco_status.evidence: Active smoker with no cessation counseling documented — smoking is the dominant modifiable barrier to arterial-ulcer healing and must be addressed.

infection_addressed.evidence: Assessed; no current signs of infection.

cases.teaching_moment: Etta's case is the one where the diagnosis is actually correct — this is an arterial ulcer, the perfusion is documented with an ABI of 0.58 and monophasic signals, and compression was appropriately withheld. It's easy to pass a chart that gets the hard part right. But three things that should be on the page aren't, and each matters on its own. There's no vascular surgery referral despite documented ischemia, and for an arterial ulcer revascularization is the actual treatment, not local dressings — without restoring flow the wound won't heal. She's an active smoker with no cessation counseling documented, and smoking is the single biggest modifiable barrier to healing an ischemic wound. And the history doesn't document any prior conservative-care trial, which the record needs to justify the plan and any escalation. None of these is a misdiagnosis; together they're a coverage record full of holes. The skill at this tier is not stopping once the etiology checks out — keep going and find every required element that's silently missing.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The etiology is right and a few elements are done correctly, which makes the chart feel solid. The difficulty is that multiple independent requirements are missing at once — vascular referral, conservative-care history, and tobacco cessation — so passing it requires auditing every criterion rather than stopping at the correct diagnosis.

patient.name: Roscoe Pennington
dx: Venous stasis ulcer, right medial gaiter area
Chronic venous insufficiency, bilateral lower extremities

radiology.finding: ABI 1.05; triphasic waveforms — no significant arterial disease

patient.wound_dressing: Multilayer compression wrap over foam primary dressing
patient.clinical_notes: 68-year-old man with chronic venous insufficiency seen for a venous stasis ulcer over the right medial gaiter area. The wound is shallow with an irregular border and a ruddy granular base, surrounded by hemosiderin hyperpigmentation and lower-leg edema — characteristic venous morphology. An ankle-brachial index of 1.05 is documented, supporting a venous rather than arterial etiology. Multilayer compression has been ordered and applied, appropriate for the ABI, and edema is being actively managed with compression and elevation. The venous diagnosis has been carried for more than three months. No venous duplex reflux study is documented to confirm the venous stasis diagnosis. No CEAP classification or VCSS score is recorded for severity or reassessment. The chart does not document a completed four-week trial of standard therapy with the specific failed interventions named. Plan: apply a cellular/tissue skin substitute at this visit.

venous_reflux_studies.evidence: No venous duplex reflux study is documented to confirm the venous stasis diagnosis — it is asserted on clinical grounds only.

abi_supports_venous.evidence: ABI 1.05 documented, consistent with venous (no significant arterial disease).

compression_appropriate_for_abi.evidence: Compression level appropriate for the documented ABI of 1.05.

edema_managed.evidence: Edema actively managed with compression and elevation.

ceap_vcss.evidence: No CEAP classification or VCSS score recorded for severity baseline or reassessment.

wound_characteristics_venous.evidence: Gaiter-area location, irregular border, hemosiderin hyperpigmentation, edema — venous morphology documented.

failed_4wk_swc.evidence: No completed four-week standard-therapy trial with specific failed interventions documented — the CTP gate is unmet despite the graft plan.

dx_over_3mo.evidence: Venous diagnosis carried for more than three months.

cases.teaching_moment: Roscoe's chart gets the most important clinical thing right: this is a venous ulcer and it's being compressed, with the compression level matched to a documented ABI of 1.05 and edema actively managed. That's real treatment, and it can make a chart feel finished. But three required elements are never established. There's no venous duplex reflux study documenting the reflux that confirms a venous stasis diagnosis — it's asserted on appearance alone. There's no CEAP classification or VCSS score, which is how venous severity is staged and reassessed over time. And most consequential for the plan, there's no documented four-week trial of standard therapy with the specific failed interventions named — that is the gate for advancing to a cellular/tissue skin substitute, so the graft planned at this visit isn't yet supported. The diagnosis is right and the compression is right; the claim still falls apart on confirmation, severity, and the CTP gate. At this tier the job is to keep auditing past the part that's done well.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The etiology is correct and the defining treatment (compression matched to ABI) is done right, which makes the chart read as competently managed. The difficulty is that multiple independent requirements are missing at once — reflux confirmation, CEAP/VCSS severity, and the four-week standard-care failure — and two of those are the CTP eligibility gate. Passing it requires checking every criterion rather than stopping at the compression.

patient.name: Velma Hardesty
patient.wound_dressing: Moisture-barrier ointment applied; foam dressing to denuded areas
patient.clinical_notes: 79-year-old woman with urinary and fecal incontinence, carried in the chart as a Stage 2 pressure injury of the buttock. On examination the patient presents with partial thickness skin breakdown is in the gluteal cleft and perianal skin and extends symmetrically onto the inner buttocks in a mirror-image pattern; it does not lie directly over the sacral bony prominence. The erythema is diffuse with ill-defined, irregular borders and blanches with pressure; the surface is moist and macerated with superficial denudation, and there is no necrosis, eschar, or distinct wound margin. She is ambulatory with assistance and repositions herself independently. A preventative pressure-redistribution mattress and a repositioning schedule have been ordered, and a nutritional assessment was completed (albumin 3.5 g/dL). The chart documents no incontinence containment or moisture-barrier protocol, and the underlying incontinence is not otherwise addressed. The breakdown is being staged and treated as a pressure injury.

stage_documented.evidence: A stage is recorded on the chart (Stage 2) — though staging is itself the error here, a stage is documented.

location_bony_prominence.evidence: The breakdown is in the gluteal cleft and perianal skin, not over the sacral bony prominence — a moisture distribution, not a pressure point.

pressure_etiology.evidence: Diffuse macerated erythema in the cleft, mirror-image, no necrosis, in a mobile patient who repositions herself — this is moisture-associated skin damage / incontinence-associated dermatitis, which per L33821 must NOT be staged as a pressure injury.

moisture_incontinence_managed.evidence: No incontinence containment or moisture-barrier protocol documented — the actual cause is unaddressed.

cases.teaching_moment: Velma's breakdown is carried as a Stage 2 pressure injury, but the chart is describing moisture-associated skin damage — specifically incontinence-associated dermatitis. Three findings give it away: the location is the gluteal cleft and perianal skin, not directly over the sacral bony prominence where pressure injuries form; the appearance is diffuse, ill-defined, blanchable, and macerated in a mirror-image pattern with no necrosis, which is moisture damage rather than a pressure injury; and the patient is ambulatory with assistance and repositions herself, which undercuts a sustained-pressure story. An MASD or IAD must not be staged as pressure injuries — staging them misclassifies the wound, and at the facility level it can wrongly inflate pressure-injury quality reporting. The treatment consequence is just as important: the orders here are pressure interventions while the actual driver, incontinence and moisture, has no containment or barrier protocol documented at all. The correct call is to recognize this isn't a pressure injury, reclassify it as MASD/IAD, and treat the moisture. Read the wound's location and character, not the label.
cases.difficulty_explanation: The front-page diagnosis is wrong and the documentation tells the truth: cleft location, blanchable macerated mirror-image morphology, and a mobile self-repositioning patient describe moisture-associated skin damage, not a pressure injury. The skill is overriding the 'Stage 2 pressure injury' label using location and etiology, and recognizing that the real cause — incontinence — is going untreated while pressure interventions are ordered.
